subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT

speakeroldname: Hon. Tom Hockin (Minister of State (Finance)) moved
subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
that Bill C-42, an Act respecting financial institutions and the deposit insurance system, be read the second time, and by unanimous consent, referred to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to begin the debate on Bill C-42. This Bill is the first of a number of Bills which will implement my new policy on financial institutions.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions

On December 18 last year, 1 tabled in the House a document entitled: New Directions for the Financial Sector, and 1 am very pleased it was so well received, both by the public and the industry.

During the last two and one-half years the federal Government was faced with a formidable challenge. It had the responsibility of formulating a policy which would, first and foremost, protect public interest and the safety of depositors. Second, we wanted to introduce a policy which would allow our Canadian financial institutions to compete in a rapidly changing global environment. The two great objectives were to protect the system and the depositors while making it a modern, global system.
I wish to begin by acknowledging the contributions of industry, other interested parties, and the public in general for their helpful suggestions and comments since the release of the Government's Green Paper on the regulation of Canadian financial institutions in April, 1985.
In addition to benefiting from our extensive consultations with the provinces and the public, we have greatly benefited from a number of major studies and reports which were prepared over the last few years. These have contributed greatly to the Government's understanding of what needs to be done in order to create a better, sounder and more competitive financial system in Canada.
In particular I commend the important contributions of the reports prepared by Justice Estey, the House, the Senate, committees of the House and the Senate, the Wyman working committee on the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation and others. In fact, this area of legislation is one of the more heavily studied areas on the Government's agenda and we have benefited very much from these studies.

I also wish to express my appreciation to representatives of the financial sector for their suggestions and comments. Mr. Speaker, I realize that the industry is anxious to see us proceed with this Bill.
Mr. Speaker, we have promised to act quickly. We want to take away much of the uncertainty concerning the implementation of the main proposals I announced on December 18 last.
Let me speak to the legislative timetable that flows from this paper. I have been concerned from the outset and have said many times that in order to draw the maximum benefit from the proposed changes we would have to move quickly to implement them. We would lose a great deal of this impact if we were to move too slowly.
I have indicated in particular that I intend to introduce the necessary legislation as quickly as possible. This will enable financial institutions to plan ahead for what is recognized to be
a period of great change in the industry-both in Canada and internationally.
Bill C-42 is the first of several legislative packages that I will be introducing over the course of the year. This Bill implements a significant part of the policy proposals, those dealing with the structure of the supervisory and deposit insurance system. It also contains measures that will enhance the protection enjoyed by Canada's depositors and insurance policyholders and promote the soundness of our financial system.
It will be followed later this spring by legislation that will reinforce existing supervisory powers and enable all types of financial institutions to own security subsidiaries.
By the summer, I hope to introduce the final package of legislation which will change institutional powers; implement the new ownership policy; establish new rules to control selfdealing and conflict of interest; and will set up the new financial institution restructuring program. That is the third and final piece of legislation that will be introduced later this spring.
Let me outline the Bill before us. The provisions of Bill C-42 primarily involve a realignment of existing regulatory agencies and a reform of the deposit insurance system. One could call this the "office Bill".
The first part of the Bill constitutes a new Act, the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions Act, which merges the Department of Insurance and the Office of the Inspector General of Banks into a consolidated regulatory agency. I expect that this new office will be better equipped to meet the regulatory challenge posed by the blurring of the distinctions between different types of financial institutions. Consolidation is necessary as a result of this blur.
The new office will continue to be funded in the same way as its two predecessors, but will have better access to qualified professional personnel by virtue of its status as a separate employer. These provisions will enable the office to hire and retain the skilled manpower that it needs to properly fulfil its regulatory responsibilities.
The office Bill also contains revised confidentiality provisions and provides for the creation of a committee of the heads of federal regulatory agencies. This will remedy a shortcoming of the existing regulatory structure, which was pointed out by Justice Estey, by facilitating the exchange of information among the new office, the CDIC, the Bank of Canada and the Department of Finance.
The second part of the Bill amends the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act in order to: first, clarify the objectives of the CDIC, notably with regard to its obligation to protect the interests of depositors; second, to enhance its ability to meet those objectives; third, to provide a more parallel treatment of federal and provincial member institutions; and fourth, to place CDIC on a more sound financial footing.
May 4, 1987

In particular, the amendments to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation Act will enhance CDIC's ability to protect depositors by providing the CDIC with the power to cancel, with ministerial approval, the deposit insurance policies of federal member institutions that violate the provisions of the Act or of CDIC's own by-laws. That power already exists with respect to provincial member institutions. As well, the amendments will levy premium surcharges on member institutions that do not follow standards of sound business or financial practice.

In addition to the power to collect additional premiums, the amendments to the CDIC Act will enable management to take a more flexible approach with respect to the establishment of premium rates. The CDIC management need these new provisions to be able to proceed with the orderly repaymewnt of their accumulated deficit. They will also enable the Governor in Council to set the annual premium rates, subject to a ceiling of one-sixth of 1 per cent of insured deposits.

As announced in a press release issued last week, I will be recommending to the Governor in Council that the current premium rate of one-tenth of 1 per cent, which has been in effect since May 1, 1985, be retained for the 1987-88 premium year. The retention of the existing rate will not result in an undue burden on deposit-taking institutions and is expected to yield sufficient revenues to amortize the current CDIC deficit over a reasonable period.
The Bill also amends a number of other Acts governing particular types of financial institutions. These include the Bank Act, the Trust Companies Act, the Loan Companies Act, insurance companies Acts and others. The changes made to these Acts will share a common purpose and can be grouped into three categories.
First, substantially revised procedures for taking control of the assets of financial institutions, or of the institutions themselves in some cases, are being implemented in order to enhance the ability of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions to protect the interests of depositors, policyholders and other creditors.
Second, responsibility for a number of essentially supervisory and administrative matters is to be transferred from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. Third,-

-the transfer from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate affairs (Mr. Andre) to the Minister of Finance of responsibility for various aspects of the incorporation of financial institutions.

Those are the three groups of miscellaneous amendments.
In conclusion, this Bill represents the first concrete steps taken toward implementing our comprehensive new policy in
Financial Institutions
the area of financial services. More important, it constitutes a major part of the changes that the Government will be introducing to improve the protection enjoyed by Canada's many depositors and policyholders, large and small, and to promote the soundness of our financial system.
My riding of London West is home to the head offices of some of Canada's finest financial institutions, including London Life and Canada Trust, to name just two. Our new policy is welcome news for them, as it is throughout the country.
Given the need for rapid implementation of these measures, I would urge the Flouse to move Bill C-42 quickly into committee.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the appearance of this Bill in the House today. It has been over a year since the House last debated a Bill pertaining to the regulation of Canadian financial institutions. That was Bill C-86, concerning the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
Of course, last November we dealt with Bill C-27 which facilitated the Hongkong Bank's takeover of the Bank of British Columbia. But that was not a regulatory Bill, it was more of a clean-up Bill to take care of a situation that had developed beyond the Government's ability to deal with. We have seen several such Bills, which only reinforces the need for the Government to get on with the process of regulatory reform.
We in the Official Opposition support the reform process. We want to see the existing legislation updated so as to have a coherent operating standard for Canadian financial institutions as they are today and as they evolve. The traditional concept of the four pillars has given way to the more recent trend to integration of services. We want Canadian institutions to be a part of the increasing internationalization of financial services and, above all, we want to ensure that the interests of consumers are well protected. The pressure for change has been coming from the industry, not from consumers, who also have their concerns about the over-all stability and solvency of the system.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT

speechtext:
I was saying, Mr. Speaker, that the pressure for change has been coming from the industry, not from consumers, who also have their concerns about the overall stability and solvency of the system as well as about the quality of service, wherever they happen to live. We want to be very sure that the Government has the interests of the consumers as well as the industry in mind when it brings forward its proposals.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
Bill C-42, as the Minister has said, is the first of a series of three Bills arising out of the White Paper tabled last December. After two and a half years and two very expensive bank failures, Bill C-42 is the first piece of legislation to come out of a process of reform which began with the previous Liberal Government.
The proposals in Bill C-42 are the least contentious of those put forward in the White Paper. There has been near, if not complete unanimity on the need to strengthen the supervisory system for federally regulated financial institutions and to make some changes in the deposit insurance system. This is essentially what Bill C-42 proposes.
The more contentious issues, such as ownership of financial institutions, expansion of their powers, prevention of selfdealing, and the role of accountants and auditors, have been left for later and there really is no excuse for this.
To begin with, we know what are the Government's intentions. We have had two sets of comprehensive proposals. We have had stacks of reports and submissions from the Commons committee on finance, Senate Banking Committee, Government appointed studies and the Estey Commission of inquiry.
The Government claims its reform process is a priority. Therefore, why after two and one half years are we not seeing action? Bill C-42 is a first step but why does the Minister not accelerate his timetable? The Minister has said that a future Bill will be an amended version of Bills C-8 and C-9. These Bills have been around since the last session. Therefore, why have we not seen it tabled in the House?
It is disconcerting to find in particular that legislation covering all the most controversial aspects of the reform scenario have no firm date for introduction. We have had all too many opportunities to see the Government's reform program go awry over the last two and a half years.
It is not as though anyone is urging the Government to keep the brakes on. On the contrary, it is my impression that the Government has industry-wide support and encouragement to get on with it. If we had all the Bills before us, we would be better able to assess them individually because we would be able to examine the parts and the whole. As it is, Bill C-42 gives us proposals for the regulatory apparatus but we will have to wait until later, possibly much later, to see exactly how this apparatus functions and who regulates what.
However, as I said at the outset, we welcome this Bill and since we are in general agreement with what the Bill proposes and have no desire for a protracted debate, my comments today will be relatively brief.
Bill C-42 corresponds roughly to Chapter 5 of the White Paper issued last December. Part I of the Bill creates a new regulatory body, the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, by amalgamating the existing office of the Inspector General of Banks with the Department of Insurance. This is consistent with what Liberal Members of the Commons
finance committee proposed in our minority report which was issued in November 1985 at the time of the finance committee's report on the Green Paper. We were not in agreement with the finance committee's proposal to establish a "mega-regulator", but we did see a need for more regulatory muscle.
I am also pleased to see that Bill C-42 proposes that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation remains separate from the regulatory body. Insuring and regulating are different functions and are probably best kept separate.
The Bill proposes that the new office be funded partly through parliamentary appropriations and partly through assessments levied on the institutions, presumably to be scaled somehow to their size. I will be interested to know how the Government plans to implement this system of levies and how it will decide what a given institution should contribute. Will the institutions themselves have any input? What if they do not agree with their assessment, will there will be any means of appeal or review? There are no answers in the Bill.
In the organization of the new office, the Bill provides for it to be a separate employer under the Public Service Staff Relations Act. This means that the superintendent may hire staff without being bound by the Public Service classification system. This is a proposal I support because it gives the superintendent the leeway to hire the kind of specialized, high calibre staff needed to inspect and monitor our financial institutions.
There is also a need for greater numbers of staff. Hon. Members will recall that at the time of the bank failures there was a certain amount of emphasis placed on the fact that the office of the Inspector General of Banks did not have the numbers of people needed for the standard of supervision required. There has since been an increase in person-year allocation for the 01GB, and with its amalgamation, of course, it will become larger. However, I would like to see some assurance that, in terms of person-years, the new office will be more than the sum of its parts.
The new superintendent is already in place as the present Inspector General of Banks. He is fortunate to enjoy the confidence of the industry as well as the Government. It would have been better if the Government had brought the Bill forward earlier for debate. However, as it is, we will do our part to see it through in reasonable time so that the new superintendent can get on with the job.
The superintendent, under the Bill, acquires new powers. There is some adjustment of the powers held by the Minister and by the superintendent. It might perhaps be said that the Bill leaves the Minister with final approval over the birth and death of an institution while the superintendent makes the decisions about what happens during its life. Put in those terms, it sounds quite cut and dried. The real test of this regime will be when an institution falls into poor health.
May 4, 1987

The existing legislation allows the regulator to take control of an institution when it can be proved that its assets are not properly accounted for. Bill C-42 would allow the regulator to assume control of an institution for seven days or longer and to make business decisions for the institution if he sees that "there exists any practice or state of affairs which may be materially prejudicial to the interests of the policyholders or creditors". Obviously this is not an action to be taken lightly or often.
I would like some definition of the terms used in this part of the Bill and a clearer idea of some of the circumstances under which the regulator would assume control of an institution. Also, according to the Bill, the regulator is not required to consult the Minister before taking this action, although it certainly would be sensible to do so. At any rate, it is something I would like to see included in the Bill. Regardless of how much good sense the regulator may have, it should be very clear that the Minister is to be kept informed.
The Bill also contains an interesting proposal to form a coordinating committee whose members would be the new Superintendent of Financial Institutions, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Chairman of the Board of the CDIC. The proposal is interesting because it actually sets out in legislation the requirements for consultation and the framework, which is this committee. This is most definitely a reaction to the gaps and breakdowns in communication which so complicated and contributed to the bank crises in 1985.
The membership of this committee is identical to that of the CDIC Board of Directors, but the function of the committee is different. The whole purpose of this new committee is to share information and advice. I approve of this goal, obviously, but it is also clear that the success of this committee as a monitoring group and consultative body will depend a great deal upon its terms of reference and the personal willingness of each of its members to make it work.
It is encouraging to note that the superintendent designate, who would chair this committee, has served notice that he intends to interpret the legislation rigorously and will not permit its members to send substitutes to committee meetings, which often happens in the case of CDIC board meetings.
The proposal as it is does not allow for industry representation on this committee, presumably on the assumption that the potential for conflict of interest would outweigh the benefits of input from people with experience and up-to-the-minute knowledge of industry conditions and trends. However, there is no doubt that the regulators need this kind of contribution, whether it is on the co-ordinating committee or a separate professional advisory group.
Bill C-42 also makes a number of substantive proposals concerning deposit insurance. Before discussing them I would
Financial Institutions
like to refer briefly to Bill C-86 which was passed about one year ago and which allowed for up to four private sector representatives on the CDIC Board of Directors. To date, not one has been appointed.
I would also mention that the practice of sending substitutes to board meetings does not sit well with me. It seems only logical that if the regulator's co-ordinating committee prohibits substitution, the CDIC board should do so as well. Substitution at private sector board meetings is unheard of. In this particular area of the public sector it should not be permitted either.
To return to Bill C-42, it proposes an increase in the premiums paid for deposit insurance by financial institutions. The current rate is one-tenth of 1 per cent of insured deposits. The Bill proposes increasing this to a maximum of one-sixth of 1 per cent. At this rate we are told CDIC's $1.2 billion deficit will be retired by 1994, assuming no more institutions fail. The Bill also proposes doubling to $3 billion the CDIC's line of credit from the Government's Consolidated Revenue Fund.
If these proposals are meant as a serious response to the CDIC deficit, then I am not satisfied. I would prefer to see the CDIC handling its deficit quite separately from normal operations. I am quite surprised at the Government's reliance in this scenario on there being no further failures of financial institutions. Even if this new regulatory system were to be successful in staving off any disasters under federal jurisdiction, the CDIC also insures provincially-regulated institutions, which have been particularly vulnerable in the years during and since the recession. So I do not think that the Government is justified in relying on wishful thinking to eliminate the CDIC deficit.
I also note that the proposals concerning CDIC do not in any way acknowledge the fact that the Government itself is partially responsible for the CDIC's deficit. This is a matter I have raised on a number of occasions. CDIC funds have been used more than once to implement decisions that were policy decisions of the Government rather than part of CDIC's mandate, for example, part of the Canadian Commercial Bank bail-out, the $200 million paid to the Hongkong Bank to take over the Bank of British Columbia and, most recently, $275 million to the Province of Alberta to restructure a couple of ailing trust companies. If government funds had been used I suppose it would have added to the deficit. But why is it more acceptable for the Government to transfer part of its deficit to the Canadian Deposit Insurance Corporation?
Another section of the Bill, Clause 71, proposes that CDIC investment, which was previously limited to the Bank of Canada, now be extended to all member institutions and to financial institutions outside Canada. I would like to know more about this. For example, what are the criteria for investment outside Canada?

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
There are other proposals concerning the CDIC which can be characterized as incentives to good business practice, or perhaps as having a stick as well as a carrot. It is proposed, for example, that CDIC have the power to terminate insurance coverage, with the approval of the Minister. CDIC has had this power relative to provincially-regulated institutions. Bill C-42 extends it to federally-regulated institutions. This is, of course, a Draconian measure since an institution cannot legally operate without deposit insurance-withdrawal of insurance forces closure.
Another new proposal would allow CDIC to levy a premium penalty on institutions deemed to be carrying out unsafe or unsound business practices. This could be risky. A premium surcharge on an institution would not force it to close its doors, but it could result in a crisis of confidence if it were to become known that CDIC was assessing penalties for substandard operating procedures. Of course, the intent is that it should not be in the public knowledge, but the question must still be addressed.
There is also the question of public knowledge versus industry knowledge. I would like to see a definition here bearing in mind the consumer's right to know in order to make intelligent decisions. 1 would also like to know how the Government defines "sound business and financial practices", the expression used in the Bill. I would like to have some idea of how it is to be interpreted relative to the risk experience of the different kinds of financial institutions.
These are matters which we can examine more deeply in committee. There is also the question of alternatives to the current system of how CDIC sets premium rates for its member institutions, if they should be risk-related or if there should be separate pools of funds for the different kinds of financial institutions. I look forward to hearing at committee about what work the Government is doing in the whole area of risk assessment.
What we have in some of the provisions in Bill C-42 is essentially a dose of preventive medicine. A number of proposals are there mainly for their value as deterrents and only to be used as a last resort and, in some cases, with concurrence by the Minister.
It is a useful first step in the process of legislating reform in the financial services sector. I regret that it has taken the Government over two and a half years to get to this point. However, I look forward to seeing the remainder of the legislation and hope that there will be no further delays in the Government's timetable.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-42 is the Government's first response in legislative terms to the problems that have been endemic, not just for a year or two and not just after the collapse of the CCB and the Northland Bank but long before that. Thus, I have a real sense that we are closing the stable door awfully late and that the over-all cost to depositors, to the institutions, and directly or indirectly to Canadians as a whole, for a while at any rate, through the
tax system, is now approaching some $2 billion. That is a great deal of money to go out the stable door.
I was recalling as the debate began on Bill C-42 how long it has been evident that there are problems in terms of the regulation of financial institutions, an issue which this Bill is intended to address. I had the opportunity to take part in the Ontario committee which reviewed the collapse of Crown Trust and which sought to review the regulation of financial institutions at the provincial level. This occurred in about 1982, a year or so after the collapse of Crown Trust and several other related companies.
At that time, one of the very sad and sorry things we learned as we looked into the operations of the Superintendent of Insurance of Ontario, who had jurisdiction over provincially chartered trust companies, as well as the Ontario Superintendent's interrelationship with the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance on the federal level, was the degree to which regulation of financial institutions was lax, slow and insensitive to the real problems. These real problems came about because of a change in practice and, I believe, a change in ethical standards on the part of people operating financial institutions.
One of the reasons Crown Trust was so easily raped and pillaged, in my view, was that the people who were there were running it like a crusty old institution for so many years and just did not know how to respond when a bunch of fast-buck operators with no ethics or morals at all sought to clean out the treasury in order to finance the flip that involved the Cadillac-Fairview buildings and Leonard Rosenberg.
The people running the trust company did not know what to do, and it is sad to say, albeit with hindsight, that they did not even know that someone should have taken their ethical principles in hand and simply walked out the door and gone to the newspapers to say that this will not do and explain what was happening before it was too late. That did not occur.
One of the things that sticks out in my mind from that particular episode is that at the time that there were questions about the financial regulation of the various trust companies involved, the discussions between the Department of the Superintendent of Insurance of Ontario and its federal counterparts was a comedy of errors. In their attempt to take effective action to stop these fast-buck artists, they found that whoever was in charge of the matter was off on a French course, or on holidays, or for some other reason had not bothered to inform the Inspector General of what was going on. A pattern like that became very obvious to us at that time.
I believe the previous Government is to be criticized as well as the present Government for not responding to that pattern, by recognizing the very grave risks that were being taken, particularly after the financial turmoil that began to occur in the market with the very sharp rise in interest rates at the beginning of the 1980s. The previous Government did not respond, and then when the new Government came into power
May 4, 1987

it inherited a situation which it should not have had to inherit, but it has tolerated that situation. Then, perhaps in the interest of winning western votes or perhaps as a preconceived notion that when the Liberals had been in power the Government was traditionally opposed and insensitive to the needs of western financial institutions, the present Government galloped to the defence of the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank in a manner which we now know led to a loss of more than $1 billion to the public through deposit insurance institutions.
That is all history. I believe it is relevant to discuss that history in discussing Bill C-42, and the other parts of the financial package the Minister has promised that we will see some time in the next month and a half or two months. I think the necessary action must involve all of the elements cited by the Minister and not just an improved pattern of regulation.
It is clear that excessive concentration in the industry is a problem. In our opinion, the Government's proposals on ownership are inadequate. It is clear that there are real problems with self-dealing, particularly in some of the smaller institutions. We do not yet know what will happen about that.
I believe there are clear danger signals in the degree to which the four pillars are being collapsed into one. The White Paper indicates that the Government more or less supports that collapse but it seems to me that we are embarking on a difficult and possibly perilous path. The new Superintendent of Financial Institutions will be charged with bringing together two organizations which did not co-operate very well in the past, and will also be responsible for this committee which will bring together the different players.
The CDIC, the Department of Finance and the Bank of Canada will get together formally in order to talk about things from time to time. If I recall, these elements did meet regularly on the Bank of Canada Board, if not elsewhere, but those meetings did not appear to be particularly fruitful. It is useful that the Bill provides for such meetings, but I think there is still the potential for human error and for the regulators to be too trusting, as they were in the past with Crown Trust, the CCB and the Northland Bank.
I took an opportunity to have a quick look at the summary of the Estey Commission inquiry. What a tragedy of errors that was. Auditors did not do the jobs for which they were being paid. I think it is bordering on the criminal that to this day there has been no effective action taken to discipline auditors who failed to notify the public, through annual reports or other means, of the situation that existed, and who consistently over a lengthy period of time tolerated the phoney devices which were being used by those two banks to make it look as though they were profitable and their balance sheets were still in order when that was not so.
The Minister knows the degree to which there was capitalization of interest taking place and the extent to which there were roll-overs upon roll-overs and work-outs upon work-outs, all in an attempt to forestall the evil day when the whole house of cards would come crumbling down. It is sad to say that the Government allowed itself to be sucked in by that.
Financial Institutions
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the then Minister of State for Finance were not perceptive enough to ask a few of the questions that should have been asked by the Governor of the Bank of Canada and by the Inspector General of Banks about the real picture beneath this Potemkin village of finance which had been created to indicate Government support should continue. Of course, it eventually collapsed and at great expense.
The reform in Bill C-42 is a consequence of, among other things, a very rapid change which has taken place in finance, not just in Canada but elsewhere as well. It is also clearly a consequence of the concerns I and many others have been raising about institutional solvency and about the fact that the standard of behaviour for people involved in the financial services industry is changing to the point where we can no longer trust the unwritten gentleman's code that ensured financial institutions remain solvent without pushing to the limit whatever powers they have. That is one of the reasons why the loosening of the statutory restraints is rather difficult to accept. The loosening of those restraints will leave more options available to press to the limit the powers which are being given to the banks, trust companies, insurance companies and the investment industry.
The Government has come up with a legislative compromise in which it is trying to both deregulate and re-regulate the system. This involves a dramatic change in the rules, the most dramatic change we have seen since the collapse of the Home Bank when the Government tried to legislate the four pillar system with which we have become familiar. The fact is that those pillars have become more and more blurred and will be even more blurred now that the Government's proposals are coming into force.
The limitations on commercial lending by trust companies will almost entirely disappear on the one hand and on the other hand, as the Minister said, the banks and other financial institutions will have the power to deal directly in the investment industry. One might argue that that is happening none too soon, given the degree to which, at another level, foreign ownership is being allowed into the investment industry.
One of the unsettling characteristics of what is happening is the emergence of a number of financial conglomerates to bring together under one corporate grouping several different financial institutions. The percentage share of closely held conglomerates with strong commercial links has been steadily advancing over the course of a few short years, and deregulation is likely to encourage this trend.
I recall in the late sixties and early seventies the degree to which the banks were able to move into consumer credit, an area which had previously been controlled by the instalment finance companies that have now effectively fallen back into being a role of minor players in this particular area. The chartered banks still control something like 70 per cent of all deposits. However, clearly their share of the deposit taking market is likely to decrease and decrease quite rapidly over a short period of time.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
I recognize that this is occurring elsewhere. Great Britain has had a big bang in which London has been encouraged to abandon most of the restraints on its financial institutions. Similar liberalization has already taken place in the United States. They have opted for deregulation, and the pressure of that deregulation is being felt here. Just a week or two ago we had contact with Dennis Elealey, a former Chancellor of the Exchequer in a Labour Government in Britain. His response was: "Watch out, Canada; be very careful about what you are doing".
Since the big bang we have seen enormous six-figure salaries, which in Britain are very big, being paid to teenage gurus and whiz kids. Well, they are not teenagers; they are only in their twenties. There has been an enormous escalation of exactly the kinds of practices of which we in Canada should be very wary.
The fact that there is a move toward globalization in financial transactions should not lead us to go willy-nilly along the directions carved by the United States and by Great Britain.
Just in the time since the White Paper appeared there has been a series of financial scandals on Wall Street in the United States which involved many of the same institutions and transactions that are intended to be governed here. The investment industry and the deposit-taking industry there have emerged with a very serious blot on their reputation. Major investment bankers like Shearson and Lehman have found themselves directly implicated. Hundreds of millions of dollars worth of frauds have been demonstrated to have occurred.
One must ask: "Is this what we are to get in Canada?" If we do so, will the Government of Canada, through the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, once again rush to the rescue of deposit-taking institutions? Once again are we to bail out institutions in which foreign depositors invested, presumably in an unregulated way, and then came with their begging cups in hand and saying: "If you do not pay us off, the reputation of the financial industry in Canada will be severely impaired"?
We bought that argument to the tune of $400 million or $500 million of payments to uninsured institutional depositors who had every reason to know better and to have expected that they should not have been compensated if they happened to have made a bad decision.
The concern about deregulation at least has had the impact of persuading the Government not to move to a total big bang. Bank failures pointed to a wide number of problems related to the regulation and supervision of institutions. It became clear that financial difficulty was frequently related to severe errors on the part of managers, to excessive risk-taking, to selfdealing, to conflict of interest, and to the mismatching of assets and liabilities.
Another area to which the Estey Commission report pointed is the failure of directors to exercise due diligence in terms of their role as the directors of banks like the Northland and the
CCB. These guys-and gals, I suppose, although they were mainly men-were being waltzed into a view of the world which bore no resemblance to reality at all. They failed to insist that management kept them adequately informed. It is my conviction that many of the directors did not even know the degree to which difficult situations had been put together with cloud-cuckoo-land financial forecasts or the degree to which those two banks, in particular, had basically papered over their deficiencies and therefore demonstrated to the directors that they were solvent at the time the two institutions were essentially bankrupt. It was not until those institutions could no longer raise capital or funds in the market that they were finally brought to book and had to be shut down.
As the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) pointed out, we have had a surfeit of public policy studies of regulation of financial institutions. We have had the Wyman report on the CDIC. We have had the Dupray task force in Ontario. We have had the reports of the Senate and Commons finance committees. The ECC has reported, and many of the recommendations we have now flow from the Estey Commission report.
All these reports concluded-and as 1 stated earlier we did not need all these reports in order to reach that conclusion- that there was a major systemic weakness in terms of the Government's ability to spot and to identify problems in unhealthy institutions and, further, to do something about those problems once they began to be identified.
I welcome the fact that many of those deficiencies are being addressed in Bill C-42. When it goes to the finance committee we will have a chance to look at them in more detail to establish whether the a's, b's, p's and q's are adequate to the kinds of needs. It is a bit difficult to comment on those right now.
However, I want to comment on one of the elements which the Government has left until later, that is, the question of the domestic ownership policy. The Minister will know that we take grave issue with the Government's decision that it will interfere in no way with the ownership of financial institutions up to the point where they reach an asset base of $15 billion, in the case of chartered banks, and something similar in the case of trust companies and insurance companies. Even then the Government will give five years for the companies to introduce an element of wider spread ownership. That element is to be limited to only 35 per cent.
In other words, an institution which is approaching the $15 billion point now will have a lengthy period of time in which it can get onside. As well it is not clear exactly what the Government would intend to do in terms of policy if an institution did not get onside by the end of five years. We know the kinds of excuses which can be made by an institution to explain why it is not prepared to do it yet.
May 4, 1987



For example one might suggest that this is not the right time, that the financial markets are not in a good position for the issue of shares to meet the objective of having 35 per cent of the shares of a trust company or a bank in the hands of the owners, except those who have control.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that the Government's proposed legislation imposes the idea that our banks and the other financial institutions be under very diversified ownership. As a matter of fact, 15 to 20 years might elapse before a new bank will establish itself and reach the level of $15 billion in assets. After that, will the regulations change? If I were responsible for the strategic planning of one such institution I would say that things change. Pressure may be brought to bear on this Minister and this Government, but for us it is not limited to this particular time.

Effectively a $15 billion rule, with the permission to continue to grow, would mean that a bank could reach $20 billion in assets and only then be subjected to a 35 per cent ownership rule. The idea that we would step in, in order to put some restraint on the large families which control so much of our trust company industry, is simply not there. They will laugh at this particular measure, indicating that it is not particularly effective.
If there is a minority shareholding, it is no guarantee that these large pools of capital will not continue to be used in the abusive way which we have seen before. When I use the word "abusive", I do so in a fairly broad context.
We had a very lengthy debate in the House last week over the plight of Canada's farmers and the problems they are experiencing. What I find unsettling is the double standard which seems to prevail when the banks come to making their loans. If a farmer tries to extend the loan because crop conditions are not good-and it is difficult to make even an operating profit in farming today-then all hell breaks loose. That farmer may well be driven to the wall and beyond, forced to have his equipment auctioned off at a pittance, the livestock sold at far less than market value, winding up with nothing after a lifetime and, in certain cases, many lifetimes in farming the same farm within the same family.
What happens in the financial sector, Mr. Speaker? What happens when Conrad Black or someone of that ilk wants to engage in some kind of corporate takeover? He calls a few friends. In no time at all a line of credit, over half a billion dollars or a billion dollars, is arranged. It is as easy as going to sign for a loan for a new car when you deal in that kind of rarefied atmosphere.
There is something wrong when people get hundreds of millions of dollars in paper entrepreneurship for this kind of paper pushing which, in many cases, is of absolutely no benefit at all to the Canadian economy or which, as we have seen now with the sorry plight of Dome, can have an extremely negative impact on our economy.
Financial Institutions
These situations create bids that go far beyond the underlying values of the assets being acquired. People can do that, making arguments about synergy and how they are going to recover the full value which the previous owners had failed to recognize, et cetera, et cetera. A lot of that is hogwash, but the banks have bought it again and again, and it is not going to end.
It will not end partially because the Government is not prepared to see widely spread ownership as the rule for any large financial institution. The Government instead is going to see a certain amount of minority holdings as a requirement. It will still leave in place the situation where the directors of these financial institutions will be drawn from a small corporate elite in Canada. The Hon. Member is shaking his head. But that is what we have right now, a small corporate elite who lunch together, perhaps at Winston's, who meet each other, who play together, who winter together in the Caribbean and who feel a commonality of interest and who are ever too ready to help a friend when a few hundreds of millions of dollars is needed to finance some kind of corporate paperpushing exercise.
On the one hand, you have the emergence in Canada of a situation where many people cannot even go to a bank because they do not have any money to open up a bank account. That is real. You have a situation where increasing numbers of Canadians are homeless and virtually destitute, where poverty is increasing. While some changes which may be useful are being made in this area, not enough is being done to break the degree to which corporate power will continue to direct the financial institutions of Canada, according to the reforms which are being put in place by a Conservative Government.
Perhaps that is not surprising. It is a Conservative Government. It has inherited a mess which was created by the Liberals but, as my leader pointed out during the course of the 1984 election campaign, comparing Liberals and Tories is like comparing Tweedledum and Tweedledee. It is like comparing Visa and MasterCharge.
When it comes to the question of whether or not the Government of Canada should be prepared to try to break up some of these pools of corporate economic power in our financial institutions, the answer we would have had from the Liberals is very similar that which we are getting now from the Progressive Conservatives, namely, they are not prepared to break up those pools of corporate power.
The Minister is waiting anxiously to find out what our opposition is to this Bill. 1 have told him what our position is likely to be on the Bill with respect to corporate ownership. We have real reservations. This Bill on its own is obviously not enough to deal with problems that also relate to powers, to self-dealing and to ownership. We will come to those later. Yes, we will support this Bill, with a number of reservations along the lines I have been putting forward, because it is clear that we need to have better Governments and better regulation than we have had.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
I still remain somewhat skeptical, and I hope the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will impose a sense of public responsibility right through his organization. I regret to say, that sense was not there before. I get angry when I see some of the abuses that have occurred in the area of financial institutions. I get so angry that I want to weep over what has taken place.
I get angry when I find out that a person, a regulator, who had a responsibility for asking questions that go underneath the bland assurances that well-fed corporate executives were giving from the banks and financial institutions, failed to do his or her job. Perhaps it is unfair to pick on regulators. They are civil servants. They are not particularly well paid perhaps compared to some of the people whose activities they are meant to be regulating. They deal in difficult circumstances. Certainly the Inspector General of Banks and his office were grossly underfunded and understaffed in the period of time about which we are talking.
I still cannot help feeling that when these abuses were taking place that surely the regulators should have been kicking and screaming. A whistle-blowing law in Canada would allow regulators to go public with what they know when they find out that inadequate action is taken by the supervisors. Had some whistle-blowing taken place, going back five or six years to Crown Trust, or more recently to the recent failures, I predict that we could have saved the CDIC a large proportion of the very large sums in which it is in deficit right now. We could have saved Canadian depositors, who eventually will pay, and borrowers who will eventually pay, the cost of the premium increases being imposed in this Bill, the great amount they are being asked to pay because of the increases in premiums. Those increases in premiums would not have been necessary. Why? Because the losses would not have occurred in such magnitude. Unfortunately, that did not occur.
I do welcome the fact that under the Bill the powers are to be greatly enlarged. The Bill responds to the Estey Commission report and the office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. Between the superintendent and the CDIC there are greater powers for going into the books. They have the power to require that an adverse report on a financial institution shall be put before the directors of that institution within 15 days. If the directors do not act, at least they cannot say "Well, we did not know", which was the case of the CCB and of Northland.
The powers of the Superintendent include the power to temporarily seize assets of a troubled institution to give officials time to respond to specific complaints about the institution's operations, such as a possible inability to handle liabilities or improper accounting of assets on the books.
Before I go conclude, Mr. Speaker, the basic question still remains. Is there the political will and is there the bureaucratic will to use those powers, greatly enhanced, which did not exist before? It is my conviction that, although the powers were limited as far as the Superintendent and the Inspector General were concerned before, in the end, if they did not have the power to act directly, those officers had the power of publicity. They had the power to issue a press release. They should not
say simply that, in our opinion we do not feel these institutions are acting according to the rules of sound financial management and, therefore, we are undertaking whatever measures available to bring those institutions into check. It is quite true that there were time delays in certain cases which would prevent them from acting immediately to safeguard what assets might remain. That is a problem. But if the Superintendent or the Inspector General had gone to the president of the CCB or of the Northland and said, "I want you to look at this draft press release. This is what I believe needs to be said in public about your institution. I happen to lack the powers to shut you down today but I intend to make this release public within a day, two days or seven days unless you take the following corrective actions", is it seriously to be believed that those institutions would seek to call the bluff if the Inspector General had shown that kind of determination? I do not believe so, Mr. Speaker.
One has to ask, what about the political level? Was it informed? Not always. However, when they were, would they have backed up that kind of action by the Inspector General? We were told a year and a half ago that the IG had contact with the then Minister of State for Finance. Unfortunately the Minister herself was unwilling or unable, did not have the competence or the experience-I am not sure what. She has emerged politically unscathed from that experience, but she is partly responsible for what went on. She could have said to the IG, "that is a mess out there, you go and stop it." That could have been done without the extra powers which are being given in this case.
If the Superintendent remains unconvinced about the solvency of an institution there can be a hearing with the Minister of Finance, after which the licence can be restricted, or the Superintendent can be directed to take over the institution for an indefinite period. If the poor practices of the institution do not change at that point the Superintendent can begin winding up procedures. It is a much better articulated system than existed before, but we saw the system fail before, even though there really were powers which could have been used to bring those institutions to account. I fear that could occur now as well.
I just want to speak briefly on the question of deposit insurance. The CDIC deficit right now stands at about SI.5 billion. Most of it is attributable, not to insured deposits but to uninsured deposits in the case of the 1985 bank failures. 1 would like the House to at least consider the question of whether there should not have been and should not now be a certain degree of co-insurance on deposits over a certain amount. 1 think for deposits up to $25,000, or something like that-a certain sum which reflects what might be held by naive and unsophisticated investors-that 100 per cent insurance makes sense. However, we have seen an escalation of insurance to the point where the entire responsibility for the fiscal management and financial rectitude of an institution rests on the regulator. There is no market pressure there at all.
May 4, 1987

My Party has trouble from time to time with people suggesting that the market is everything. 1 have trouble, conversely, as a democratic socialist in a semi-capitalist economy, with suggestions made by the Government which effectively say that there should be no market pressure at all. If you had a 10 per cent or 20 per cent co-insurance feature on deposits over $25,000 or $30,000, let us say up to $100,000 or something like that, and an institution failed, the depositors run the risk of losing up to 10 per cent or 15 per cent of their deposit. It seems to me that that would ensure that high flying financial institutions, behaving the way too many have behaved over the course of the last two years, would have their wings trimmed. People with large sums to invest would be extremely wary about getting an extra half per cent interest from an institution that was not investing prudently, taking unwarranted risks with the money.
In other words, the market itself would prevent those institutions from growing as rapidly as the CCB and the Northland Bank were able to grow. It would prevent the kind of situation where institutions grow like Topsy and where the risk relative to public deposit insurance grows to the levels we have seen.
The Government claimed at the time it had no choice but to bail out those two western banks. It made certain assurances, and I think Governor Bouey may have been partly responsible for that. It may well be that no matter what level of deposits are formally insured, future Governments may also find themselves in that same box. I would hate to see that.
I am lectured to and preached at about the market system from time to time, but when we turn around, as we did at the time of the CCB affair, and say let the market system prevail and make those guys take what they can get when the institution is wound up, we were told no, that is not to be.
I would suggest that if the principle is in place that there be a certain amount of co-insurance on deposits over a modest level, not only will that ensure that depositors whose deposits are 90 per cent insured would look carefully at the quality and character of the institution in which they place their deposits, it will also set a precedent so that uninsured depositors putting commercial deposits into those institutions will also expect that in the event of failure, even if they come with their begging cup, 10 per cent or 15 per cent of their investment will not be returned. They, too, will therefore not abuse the taxpayers of Canada through the CDIC the way those depositors did two years ago with the results we know.
1 could go on for some time, but it is the position of the NDP that the problem of financial institution solvency can be resolved only through a combination of clear and effective regulation and supervision of Canada's financial system along with strict domestic ownership limits which ensure that institutions are widely held. We have supported much of what Mr. Justice Estey advocated with respect to regulatory changes but we note that the best federal supervision available
Financial Institutions
will fail if commercial financial cross-ownership is permitted. Because the Conservatives did not introduce 10 per cent ownership limits for all financial institutions, the new regulatory authority that Bill C-42 introduces may find itself with an increasingly impossible job on its hands in the years ahead.
As I have just suggested, we could also put some of that responsibility in the hands of any investors who have more than modest sums to invest so that they, too, keep an eye on the rectitude and solvency and management practices of the institutions in which they put their funds.
