subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure for me to rise and speak on Bill C-42.
Speaking as a member of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs, we spent a great deal of time on this subject over the last two to three years. I first want to commend and compliment the Minister of State for Finance (Mr. Hockin). I can recall, a few days after he was appointed, consulting with him and asking if he would be moving quickly on the various studies which had already been done. My thought there was that the last thing we needed was another study. 1 was very impressed with his remarks. He said he would be getting on with the job just as quickly as possible, and he has been true to his word.
I am going to deal with just the supervisory reform and changes to the CDIC. I have full confidence that the other measures concerning ownership and so on will be dealt with shortly. I think it would be useful to refresh our memories a little bit about some of the comments made in the studies. I will just refer to the committee report which begins with supervisory reform.
Recent trends and problems in the Canadian financial system have highlighted the need to improve the federal supervisory system. The failure of seven federally-supervised financial institutions during 1985, two chartered banks, three trust companies and two property and casualty insurance companies raises serious doubts about the adequacy of the supervisory system. Failures of provincial institutions, while not the direct responsibility of federal supervisory authorities, also underline the need for improved supervisory standards across all jurisdictions.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
In his testimony before the committee the Superintendent of Insurance cited the numerous reasons for the failure of seven federal trust and mortgage loan companies and four property and casualty companies. These include inadequate capital, over-exposure in real estate, low quality mortgages with questionable appraisals, mismatching between assets and liabilities, abusive self-dealing, the use of unlicensed reinsurers, and the poor quality of management.
In its study of the circumstances leading up to the support package provided to the CCB in March, 1985, the committee also identified a number of serious shortcomings, such as lax regulatory supervision, questionable accounting practices, inadequate disclosure, inadequate performance by outside auditors, and their lack of communication with the office of the Inspector General of Banks.
Technology accounts for another reason for supervisory reform. Computers and communications technology have enabled the financial institutions to effectively leap over traditional domestic and international supervisory boundaries. No longer is it sufficient to limit supervision to the activities of an institution in a limited geographic area. Technology, coupled with increased product deregulation and the blurring of industry boundaries, requires a new approach to supervision, one which recognizes the national and international dimensions of many financial institutions and the need to utilize up-to-date computer-based technology and modernized supervisory approaches to deal with the dramatically different financial scene of the 1980s.
A third area of reform relates to the adequacy of the supervisor's power to deal with problem situations. There is evidence from recent financial institution failures that federal regulators require additional remedial powers to perform more effectively. Also it would appear that they have not fully utilized their existing powers, or done so in a timely manner. Recent events would indicate that the traditional gentlemen's approach to financial supervision is no longer appropriate in an environment of increased risks, frequent and significant economic shifts, and intense competition. A more assertive supervisory approach is required, together with the requisite enforcement powers to get the job done. The traditional reactive mode of supervision must give way to a pro-active mode.
The supervisory process of Canadian banks has been patterned on the British system which relies heavily on institutional self-regulation and the use of outside auditors. Until 1975 the OIGB had under five employees. In contrast to the American supervisory system which employs hundreds of government examiners to perform detailed on-site examinations, the Canadian approach relies on the work of internal
inspections and external audits and generally limits its own reviews to an examination of the adequacy of bank management and the controls it has introduced to comply with prudential policies and regulations.
In contrast, the supervision of trust and insurance companies involves detailed on-site examination by federal supervisors and is much closer to the American banking scene. Both the adequacy of banks supervisory methods and responsibility of outside advisers to all financial institutions, including auditors, appraisers, actuaries and lawyers, are in need of review and revision.
The internationalization of the Canadian financial system, in particular the growing importance of foreign markets to Canadian chartered banks, life insurance companies, and some of the larger trust companies, points to the need for careful reexamination of the adequacy of present supervisory practices in the international area.
Finally, the increased blurring of differences between financial industries, particularly among the deposit-taking institutions, and the pressure from all financial industry groups for further product deregulation, reinforces the need to reexamine the suitability and effectiveness of two separate federal supervisory bodies and a separate deposit insurance entity. The shortcomings of the present organization structure were recognized in both the Green Paper and the Wyman report.
It is clear that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) not only read our report in great detail but acted very much along the lines of the recommendations that we made concerning supervision. He also had to contend with and think about other remarks and suggestions, and I would like to quote a couple from the Senate Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. They were rather cautious in their approach to this subject. For instance, they stressed the following points:
-first, to ensure that primary regulators have adequate technological and human resources to undertake effectively the monitoring and examining role under their existing powers;
-second, to enhance these powers where circumstances warrant; and
-third, to alter their monitoring procedures so that an effective early warning system is put in place and to establish a network of communication and information flow to and from the other partners in the over-all process of regulating consumer protection and institution solvency.
They make further recommendations including No. 16 which says:
To a considerable degree, the recent problems in the financial sector appear to reflect not so much an inadequate range of regulatory powers as an inadequate exercise of existing powers. To the extent that this is the case, it is important that legislators do not react to recent events by endowing regulators with unnecessary and unwarranted powers.
You can see, Mr. Speaker, that the Minister chose not to take that particular advice. I think he was correct in that.
May 4, 1987

Recommendation No. 17 says that increases in regulatory powers should be restricted to those areas where existing powers limit the ability to monitor the soundness and solvency of an institution or to restore problem institutions to financial health. They should not be utilized to supplant management's prerogative to manage and direct as an institution. The most serious weakness of the existing regulatory framework is the lack of procedures or mechanisms to identify problem institutions on a timely basis.
They go on to talk about an early warning system which I believe is a very vital area that is certainly lacking in the existing system.
On a number of occasions we made the point about where these supervisors should be located. We were dismayed to learn that literally all of them are located right here in the capital. The odd financial institution is headquartered here, but most of them are obviously in metropolitan centres like Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver. In order to have an effective early warning system your men and women should be out in the field where they can pick up on rumours about loans and so on.
I will just touch on another very thorough document which was completed by Justice Estey. He outlined five different alternatives for the structure of bank supervision. No. 3 is worded as follows:
Establish a super-regulatory agency with jurisdiction over banks, insurance companies, and trust and loan companies as recommended by the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs.
The fifth choice which this report puts forth reads as follows:
Combine the Inspector General's supervisory functions with the CD1C, which, as the insurer of the public's deposits, would determine its exposure to risk by its own supervisory activities.
1 believe that the Minister of State for Finance correctly rejected that recommendation with regard to supervisory steps, but it is clear that not only has he consulted widely with the industry, he also did not allow these reports to gather dust. They were read and culled through. I believe he grafted together legislation including the best and brightest ideas from the various studies previously done.
Bill C-42 clearly shows that the Government is committed to strengthening its ability to supervise financial institutions as part of a comprehensive policy of reform in the financial sector. The principal measures in the Bill are the consolidation of the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance into a new office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions and modifications to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. The new office will have full supervisory responsibilities for federal banks and non-bank financial institutions.
I am sure you are aware, Mr. Speaker, of how that sector is growing. In 1967 there were 223 companies. By 1984 that had grown dramatically to 352 institutions.
Financial Institutions
The CDIC will continue to be a separate entity. This will allow the retention of private sector expertise on the CDIC's board of directors. Moreover, it will preserve the CDIC's established relationship with provincial regulators.
This Bill will also provide detailed grounds on which the Government may take control of a financial institution. The existing provisions do not allow regulators to take timely and decisive action to protect the interests of depositors, policyholders, or general creditors.
Bill C-42 also addresses the issue of CDIC funding by permitting a more flexible mechanism for setting premium rates. As a result of the failure of a number of financial institutions, the CDIC had a deficit of $1.2 billion at the end of 1986.
Bill C-42 reflects the measures outlined in the December, 1986 White Paper, New Directions for the Financial Sector. These measures are based on extensive discussion and consultation. They address concerns raised in the Estey report on the Northland and Commercial banks, the Wyman report on the CDIC, and the reports of the finance committees of the House of Commons and the Senate.
Separate legislation introduced as part of the Government's reform of the financial sector will further enhance existing supervisory powers, permit the Government to review and block large transfers of ownership if necessary. It will improve solvency standards, control self-dealing and conflict of interest, and permit financial institutions to offer a wider variety of service to their clients.
Bill C-42 establishes the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions. This office will combine the operations of the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance. The office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will be treated as a separate employer under the Public Service Employment Act, thus providing more flexibility in setting classification standards and pay scales that would otherwise be impossible. This will facilitate the recruitment and retention of qualified personnel from the private sector.
The office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will be funded by assessments levied on the financial institutions under its supervision. The precise assessment formula will be set out in regulations and resemble the formula currently used to fund the Department of Insurance. The office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions will be able to spend its assessment revenue without the requirement of parliamentary appropriations.
Bill C-42 establishes a committee consisting of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, the Chairman of the CDIC, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, and the Deputy Minister of Finance. This will enable an adequate flow of information among regulatory agencies. We noted that this was certainly a problem and an issue in some of the failures that were examined.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
Bill C-42 provides detailed grounds on which the Government may take control of a financial institution and will standardize these procedures. This will further protect depositors, policyholders and other creditors when financial institutions appear to be insolvent or fail to comply with regulatory procedures.
Responsibility for major decisions affecting the birth and winding up of financial institutions will be transferred to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Some responsibilities, such as issuing letters patent, will be transferred from the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Andre), while others will be transferred from the Governor in Council. Certain responsibilities of an administrative or supervisory nature will be transferred from the Minister of Finance to the new Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
Powers of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will include measures in Bill C-42 that will strengthen the CDIC's ability to protect the interests of depositors and other creditors. The CDIC will have the power to levy premium surcharges on financial institutions which violate CDIC by-laws.
Federally incorporated financial institutions will no longer be automatically insured. They will be required to apply for insurance as is presently the case for provincially-incorporated institutions.
At present, the CDIC may terminate, through a phased process, deposit insurance coverage of a provincial member institution for unsound business or financial practices.
The CDIC will be given the power to initiate a process for termination of insurance coverage for deposits in both federal and provincial institutions. The Minister's authorization will be required before coverage of federally-regulated institutions is terminated. This would apply only to new deposits; existing deposits would continue to be insured.
Let us turn to the financing of the CDIC. This Bill will provide greater flexibility in establishing the premiums that the CDIC charges financial institutions. Effective May 1, 1987, the Governor in Council will be able to charge fees of up to one-sixth of 1 per cent of insured deposits. The rate that is established within this ceiling will reflect the need to reduce the deficit of the Deposit Insurance Fund over a reasonable period of time.
Legislation passed in 1986, which was Bill C-86, temporarily increased premiums from one-thirtieth of 1 per cent to one-tenth of 1 per cent for the period February 1, 1986, to April 30, 1987.
The minimum fee for deposit insurance will be increased from $500 to $5,000. The maximum amount which CDIC may borrow from the Consolidated Revenue Fund will be increased from $1.5 billion to $3 billion.
In closing, I am very supportive of the measures that are contained in Bill C-42. I spent a number of years in the financial services sector before seeking election and I can attest to the soundness of these provisions. They are much needed.
Canadians can be very proud of the record of our financial institutions over the long term. We have a number of world
class banks and life insurance companies and these measures today will help not only the smaller institutions but the larger ones remain sound and competitive in a world that is changing so fast.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a question for my friend who is also a colleague on the finance committee. It concerns the interrelationship between regulation and ownership restrictions. I realize that this is not directly part of the Bill, but it is certainly relevant. Does he believe that it is adequate to require only a minority interest in large financial institutions to be widely held, and whether it is adequate to give five years to banks or financial institutions to achieve that wide ownership of 35 per cent? Is it adequate only to require that kind of distribution of share ownership after institutions reach a level of assets of approximately $15 billion? Will this not simply allow continued concentration in financial markets which has been one of the causes of the problem of overconcentration in the Canadian economy and a concentration of economic power in too few hands?

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the Hon. Member for his question. As he indicated, we are colleagues on the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs. We are not dealing with a theoretical world, but a financial world which has grown in different ways for decades and we cannot simply apply some theoretical measures.
Certain companies in the trust industry have had problems over the years. Some would not be alive and thriving today if one of the major shareholders had not had the financial resources to help that company through a difficult period.
I think there are conditions by which some of these institutions should enjoy stronger ownership, with a higher percentage of ownership from certain people. However, when indeed they do increase to a certain level, then I believe the ownership level should be decreased.
The Hon. Member will recall that the finance committee suggested a graduated scale on ownership so that when the assets hit a certain level the concentrated ownership would start to diminish. We may want to revisit that particular proposal when we deal with the final legislation.
However, in general, I support the measures that were put forth. As the Member delves into the history of the survival and support of some of our trust companies, particularly regional ones which are important, he will see the virtue in the approach.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, perhaps I can pursue this briefly. It seems contradictory that on the one hand the Government ownership proposals will continue to insist that the banks be widely held and impose a limit of 10 per cent on the ownership in any single hand, while at the same time it will permit the trust company to be directed and controlled, not just by one set of interests but by an individual owner. Assets of $15 billion, $20 billion or $25 billion could effectively be under the majority control of only one owner, whether or not 35 per cent of the shares are widely held. Nonetheless, the power of discretion goes into just one set of hands.
May 4, 1987

Because of the pattern of ownership in the trust companies now, we know that is a very real possibility. It seems to me the Government has a choice. It could take the banking model and apply that to the trust industry or it could do that which it has done, which is to simply go with the flow and accept this degree of monopoly ownership of the second major group of financial institutions in the country. Surely it would have been better to have sought-although it might have taken a bit of time-a broad ownership of those trust companies, so that we achieve that, and begin to achieve that now.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Well, Mr. Speaker, one of the tragedies the country went through with the financial institutions in 1985 was the collapse of two regional banks. I, for one, was dismayed, not just because of those two particular banks, but that it likely signalled the end, certainly for a while, of the creation of regional banks. We have a very fine banking system in this country. We have five huge banks. However, I sometimes wonder how well some of the regions are being served, particularly small businesses in many regions. Perhaps a future role for some of these smaller trust companies will be to fill that vacuum.
These companies normally require someone with financial resources or partners, and if some of these smaller trust companies are formed to take up that slack, I think that is a worthwhile thing to do.
We are not a Party which puts forth retroactive legislation. As I said in my first reply, there were certain companies in place whose survival was dependent from time to time on large injections of capital. When we look over the whole scene today, I think we have a relatively healthy and vibrant financial service sector and with measures such as the increased supervision and strength of this new office, and with the other measures which are going to be coming on, we will continue to have a sound system and one of which we can be proud.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is also directed to my colleague on the committee on finance. As the Hon. Member knows, during our hearings we had some concern regarding what type of regulations we could put on the institutions and what type of effective mechanisms the regulators could have on the institutions they were regulating. It often seemed to us on the committee that the instrument available to the regulators was either the sledge hammer, taking away the licence, or not being able to do very much about abuses they were seeing. The committee found this to be an unacceptable situation, because it did not allow degrees of punishments and penalties.
I wonder if the Hon. Member would comment on how Bill C-42 would deal with the concern of the committee that the regulators would have various instruments to use with which to enforce the regulations?

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to reply to my colleague on the same committee. We worked side by side for a long time on this issue. I think the main power which will ensue from Bill C-42-and I am speaking of the supervisory area-if I could sum it up in one word, is "knowledge". I understand we are going to have more people in that department. I hope they follow the strategy we suggested, with many of them being in the field where they could avail themselves of the rumours on the street.
It is a fact that people know of an institution turning down a loan for certain reasons, such as the criteria not being met. You would be amazed, Mr. Speaker, how the financial institutions people know a month later which institution booked that deal which could have been a lot less than just marginal-perhaps even a very poor deal. But rumours are out there as to what company or institution actually booked what deal.
Therefore, knowledge is going to be power, in terms of knowing early on that interest is being capitalized, that the accounting procedure is being abused, and the knowledge of the rolling over of loans by a renewal procedure that simply covers up the delinquency of different loans. That is the real power, the talent of the people we are going to have and the knowledge they will gain from the hands-on review, and the whole system, if I could put it that way, of being out there in the field really knowing what is going on and not sitting in some ivory tower here in the capital.

subsubtopic: MEECH LAKE AGREEMENT-QUESTIONS ASKED BY LEADER OF THE OPPOSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) was right when he expressed last Friday a number of important concerns about the Meech Lake Agreement on the Constitution. For instance, our Leader asked what would happen to a national program should limitations on spending power become a reality. Medicare is one example that comes to mind. Would we have today medicare across the nation in rich and poor provinces alike if we had had in the early sixties limitations on spending power that the Government and the provincial premiers agreed upon so hastily last week?
What will happen to social programs we are now considering for implementation across Canada such as the day care policy? Will some provinces, if non-participation in national shared-cost programs becomes a reality, be saying: "No, thank you, but give us the money"? Will this money once it reaches a provincial treasury be fully used for the purpose it was originally intended? Will we have as a result provinces with low standards of day care services?
These are just a few questions that come to mind on one subject alone when wondering about the reasons why federal spending powers should be limited. Canadians want to know. They also want to be consulted.

subsubtopic: IMPORTANCE OF FOREST INDUSTRY TO PRAIRIE PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, most people envisioning Canada's prairie provinces think of vast expanses of wheat fields and herds of cattle. Some think of our black gold, the coal, oil and gas reserves of Alberta and Saskatchewan, or of the hydroelectric potential of Manitoba. Too few recognize the scope and importance of what one might call our green gold, the forest resources of these provinces.
Five pulp or paper mills, and a host of other primary product-producing manufacturing facilities, produce an array of products, including medium-density fibreboard and oriented strand board panels, laminated beams and roofing shingles. Hundreds of wood-based secondary manufacturing plants further contribute to a strong forest-based industry throughout the region.
Nearly 30,000 jobs across the Prairies can be attributed directly or indirectly to this industry. Furthermore, the value of shipments from the three prairie provinces and the Northwest Territories amounts to $1.5 billion annually.
This week marks National Forest Week in Canada. This week is an opportunity to reflect upon the important contribution of our forests to Canada. The forests of the prairie provinces hold one of the keys to the economic diversification of what is sometimes referred to as the bread basket of the nation.

subsubtopic: PARTICIPATION OF ETHNOCULTURAL COMMUNITIES IN CANADIAN SOCIETY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Parliament adopted a policy of multiculturalism within a bilingual framework 15 years ago last fall. But this policy has never been expressed in an Act such as the Official Languages Act. Successive Ministers responsible for multiculturalism have had pathetically little money to meet the needs of Canada's ethnocultural communities. The Board of Presidents of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council expressed its concern about this and other shortcomings in meetings today with all three Parties.
In this era of the Charter of Rights and Freedoms Canada requires strong leadership to ensure full participation in Canadian society by the members of every ethnocultural community and full participation of each community as a whole. Multicultural policy needs to foster the social and cultural potential of every community and to open Canadian society to the abilities of every member of these communities.
This is a time for action. The Minister needs to do far more than propose a few amendments to the Citizenship Act.

subsubtopic: CANADIAN FOODGRAINS BANK-ASSISTANCE TO PEOPLE IN NEEDY COUNTRIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Foodgrains Bank is a philanthropic organization which accepts donations of cash and grain in Canada and distributes grain to needy countries. The organization helps people stay alive through "food for work" programs by paying people grain for working on projects such as road building, reforestation and water storage development.
Through projects such as these people are paid six to eight pounds of grain for a day's work. This not only takes care of their short-term needs; the projects ensure them a better life in the long run.
Not only should the Foodgrains Bank be commended but the farmers of western Canada should be commended as well. In 1986 alone farmers from Manitoba, Saskatchewan and
May 4, 1987

Alberta donated over $850,000 worth of grain. This, in turn, was matched on a three-to-one ratio by the Government of Canada.
The Canadian Foodgrains Bank, the farmers of western Canada and the Government of Canada should be congratulated on this achievement.

subsubtopic: NEED FOR GREATER ACCESS TO HIGHER STUDIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the quality of our post-secondary education is worsening and becoming ever less accessible to people from underprivileged circles. The increase in tuition fees as well as in living and accommodation costs, the inadequacy of student aid programs, the massive indebtedness, and high unemployment among students are as many factors which make our system ever less accessible.
Ever more student aid is given in the form of loans rather than grants, with the result that students are getting ever deeper into debt. For many students the high cost of studies is often an excuse to quit school after the secondary level. We all agree that when tuition fees go up students from low-income families must obtain adequate financial assistance to make up for cash shortages. In addition, the rules governing the repayment of fees must be changed and the fees reduced so that more students can be accommodated.
We must also ensure that adults, native people, the handicapped and the poor have fair access to higher education. All these measures must be taken if we really want to give a fair chance to any student anxious to complete higher studies regardless of his or her status or social level.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO ORDER OF CANADA RECIPIENT, HARRY GAIREY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week at Rideau Hall, 74 outstanding Canadians were presented with the Order of Canada. Among the scientists, artists, athletes, charitable workers and former provincial premiers was a 92-year-old black Canadian named Harry Gairey.
Born in Jamaica, Harry came to Canada in 1914. He worked along with Lincoln Alexander's father at one of the only jobs available to blacks in Canada until recently, as a railway porter. He helped to organize the Porters' Union, the
Universal Negro Citizenship Association and the Universal Negro Improvement Association. He was a moving force in the development of credit unions and played a significant role in changing Canada's immigration laws.
For many years he has been the official greeter, information centre, compassionate friend and battler against discrimination known to all as the "Black Godfather of Metropolitan Toronto". Last week at Rideau Hall, there was Harry taking his rightful place among the movers and shakers of our society. This is truly what Canada is all about.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO ORDER OF CANADA RECIPIENT, HARRY GAIREY
speechtext: Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, today the Board of Presidents of the Canadian Ethnocultural Council is meeting in Ottawa. One of its concerns is the failure of the Conservative Government to bring forward changes promised over a year ago to the Canadian Human Rights Act to include a requirement for reasonable accommodation.
The Supreme Court of Canada decision in Bhinder was described by the head of the Canadian Human Rights Commission as devastating to those with disabilities and to ethnic and religious minorities, including Sikhs. The Commission submitted a unanimous special report to Parliament in February, 1986, calling upon the Government to require employers to accommodate differences where reasonably possible. The UN Human Rights Commission is now examining a complaint against Canada in this area.
I therefore call upon the Government, along with the Ethnocultural Council and the Human Rights Commission, to stop stalling on these important amendments to the Canadian Human Rights Act and to stop betraying its promise to Canada's disabled and ethnic and religious minorities.

subsubtopic: TRIBUTE TO ORDER OF CANADA RECIPIENT, ELIZABETH LEFORT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week, Elizabeth LeFort, a Cape Breton artist, was made a member of the Order of Canada. She was born in Point Cross, Nova Scotia, in 1914 and is a descendant of a small group of Acadians who escaped from Grand-Pre, Nova Scotia, in 1755. For more than 21 years she has established and maintained an entire gallery of hand-hooked tapestries. Thousands of tourists from all over have come to see her work.

May 4, 1987
Elizabeth LeFort has been a strong proponent of Acadian culture for many decades. She adapted the famous Acadian rug-hooking into an art form and for many years maintained an entire gallery of hand-hooked tapestries of scenes prominent in North American history, thereby contributing to the preservation of the Acadian culture and heritage.
She also completed portraits of many world leaders. She completed a portrait of Pope Pius XII, and a portrait of President Eisenhower which was presented by her upon invitation to the President in the White House in 1957. She completed a portrait of Queen Elizabeth which was also personally delivered to the Queen. She completed a portrait of President John F. Kennedy which was personally presented to him in Phoenix, Arizona, in 1961, and she completed portraits of Prime Minister Diefenbaker and Prime Minister Trudeau.
She was born on an Acadian farm in Cape Breton, and as a young girl, she learned this famous art form. She continues to teach this art to future generations. All Nova Scotians are proud of this great artist and want to express their congratulations to her.

Over the weekend, Mr. Speaker, we were saddened to hear about the premature death of Mr. Raymond Blais, the long-time president of Quebec's Mouvement des caisses populaires Desjardins. In that capacity Mr. Blais played a leading role in the socio-economic development of Quebec and Canada through the Desjardins co-operative movement. subsubtopic: CALL FOR REPRESENTATION OF TERRITORIES AT FORTHCOMING FIRST MINISTERS' CONFERENCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was welcome news when we heard last Friday that the First Ministers had come to a tentative arrangement for Quebec's participation in the Constitution.
We cannot, however, forget that there are still thousands of Canadians living north of sixty who do not today enjoy the same political rights as their southern neighbours. The Territories must be represented at the forthcoming First Ministers' Constitutional Conference since their goals and desires of becoming equal members of the Canadian partnership are directly affected by the Section 42 amending formula.
With the resolution of the Quebec situation, it is now time to redouble our efforts to bring true provincehood to the Northwest Territories and Yukon Territory.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR COMMITMENT TO FIVE-YEAR SUBSIDY SCHEME
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, a lifetime of working as a prairie farmer has trained me to look realistically at hard times and difficult situations.
I watched the Government announce grain price declines last year and again this year of 18 per cent to 20 per cent each year, and I know that farm incomes will be woefully inadequate. The Government will not commit itself to further funds at this point but says that the solution to farm price problems lies in international negotiations.
Ultimately that is the solution which Canadian farmers seek, but realistically how long will such action take? About a year ago Canada raised the question of grain pricing at the OECD meeting and apparently has agreement to have the issue on the agenda of the GATT talks. It has set up and become part of the Cairns Group.
In none of these initiatives do we have any commitment by the Americans or the Europeans, the chief people involved, to take part in the talks. They are not even part of the Cairns Group.
What Canadian farmers need is a commitment like the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise) gave to dairy producers to be part of a farm subsidy scheme for five years so that our producers know, as their European and American counterparts know, that the Government is behind them.
May 4, 1987

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Polish community observed the anniversary of the signing and ratification of the Polish Constitution of May 3, 1791, a day which is cherished by freedom-loving Poles throughout the world.
In Poland celebrations of the event were marked by the arrest of 200 Poles, serving as a reminder that the struggle for liberty and justice continues despite the efforts of those who would deny freedom's call.
Fundamental democratic principles, including freedom of expression and association guaranteed under the Constitution of 1791, have yet to be implemented in Poland. The official visit by our Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) will provide an opportunity for the Canadian Government to press Polish officials for much needed reform in the area of human rights.
As a free and democratic people, let us join with Canadians of Polish origin in commemorating and honouring the democratic principles embodied in the Constitution of 1791.

Mr. Speaker, it is remarkable how easily and quickly the First Ministers were able to strike a new constitutional deal on expanding provincial powers. The vague and uncertain concept of Quebec as a distinct society was agreed to. Where were those provincial voices asking what does this really mean? How will this distinctiveness be exercised in practice?
Contrast that, Sir, with the Premiers' reluctance and hesitation on the issue of aboriginal self-government. Here there was precision. Here there were specifics. Nothing was vague or uncertain because the scope of the right to aboriginal self-government was to be achieved through negotiations. Yet a succession of First Ministers' Conferences, held in public, achieved next to nothing.
Contrast that, Sir, with the private tete-a-tete at Meech Lake, which will have the effect of significantly altering the very nature of Canada as we know it today. Thus, there is one approach taken in the name of provincial rights, and there is quite a different one for the recognition of aboriginal rights.

subsubtopic: RESULT OF FIRST MINISTERS' MEETING-SUPPORT FOR MEECH LAKE ACCORD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last Friday many Members of the House, including the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) and the Leader of the New Democratic Party (Mr. Broadbent), celebrated with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) his success in having all provincial premiers agree to principles for amending our Constitution and for guaranteeing for Quebec, after years of uncertainty, its rightful place in Canada.
I believe that this Accord will also be welcomed by English speaking Quebecers. The Meech Lake Accord calls for recognition of the existence across Canada of linguistic minorities. It notes that they are a fundamental characteristic of our country, and it calls for Parliament and all provincial legislatures to preserve this national characteristic.

Mr. Speaker, Canada stands prouder.

All Canadians should be celebrating.

Mr. Speaker, today I join in celebrating Israel's 39th anniversary, a state that represents the fulfilment of an age-old dream of the Jewish people for a homeland. From the time Lester Pearson played such an important role in the formation of Israel to the present, Canadian political leaders have consistently supported Israel's existence as an independent and secure state.
I am pleased that all three of our political Parties remain committed to this basic belief. This support is vital at a time of continued external threats to Israel.
No one needs to be reminded that the situation in the Middle East remains volatile. There are deep divisions and seemingly insurmountable obstacles to lasting peace. We must not despair if people of good will continue to work toward the goal of peace.
It is a shocking statistic that of the 150 or so member states of the United Nations, only about 26 are true democracies. Two of them are Canada and Israel. Democracy, liberty and justice are the foundations for the unshakeable commitment that exists between our two countries. Hag Sameach to Israel.

May 4, 1987
Oral Questions MULTICULTURALISM

Mr. Speaker, today's meeting with the three political Parties by the Canadian Ethnocultural Council was important from a substantive viewpoint but also from a symbolic one in terms of heightening the awareness and importance of our national multiculturalism policy here in Parliament.
There are many challenges facing the national multiculturalism policy but three stand out. First the need to strengthen the legislative base and the departmental structuring of the Department through a multiculturalism map that was introduced by the former Government and administration, which died on the Order Paper. The present Government has failed to reintroduce it for this Parliament's consideration.
Second, the challenge is for us to define for our younger generation Canadians, the second, third, and fourth generations of various ethnocultural backgrounds, their definition of multiculturalism which will be different from their parents and grandparents' because it must address the social, the economic and the other fabrics that make this country what it is.
Third, we need to keep an open and progressive policy on immigration and refugees. If we can do this as a country, we will be sending a strong signal that Canada is open and has only one class of citizenship, namely, first class citizenship for one and all.

Mr. Speaker, we hope we can take some encouragement from that response, Mr. Speaker.
The Prime Minister knows that now, after the Accord which was signed at Meech Lake, the unanimous consent of the provinces and Parliament will be necessary for any change to the Senate. In fact, I would suggest to him that Senate reform has been placed in a constitutional strait-jacket.
Does the Prime Minister agree that he has made an elected Senate, such as requested by some of his provincial homo-logues, particularly Messrs. Getty and Vander Zalm, virtually impossible?

Not unless you want to make the assumption, Mr. Speaker, that the First Ministers are incapable of coming together in good faith to resolve matters of this kind. Premier Getty, the strongest proponent of a Triple-E Senate, felt this was very much in keeping with his desires and not something that would hobble his intentions. It was supported by all other First Ministers.
I suppose the question concerning unanimity might very well be the following. By way of illustration, if you are going to create a new province or series of provinces, is that not important enough to warrant the unanimous approval of all other provinces? Can anyone conceive of new provinces being created without the approval of the Province of Ontario or, in my judgment, the Province of Prince Edward Island? Because it changes the structure of federalism and the kind of country we have, I think it is not unreasonable to ask all existing provinces for their approval. This is very much consistent with everything I set out on behalf of my Party on August 6 in Sept-Iles regarding renewed Canadian federalism.

The Prime Minister is not historically correct when it comes to Newfoundland in 1949. Under the present constitutional provisions, seven out of the 10 provinces with 50 per cent of the population and the Parliament of Canada could approve any change in the Senate.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have a few questions concerning the constitutional accord. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought it was regrettable that the First Ministers, myself included, missed the opportunity to settle the native issue during the federal-provincial conference held barely a few weeks ago. As far as I am concerned, notwithstanding the fact that this series of constitutional initiatives has come to a close, it does not end our responsibility to seek a fair and equitable settlement to the problem of the aboriginal people in Canada. At the appropriate time I intend to review the process with the Premiers in the hope that, as it should be, we might find a formula which will do justice to the native people of Canada.

May 4, 1987
Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, at the last conference which took place on this subject, the native leaders expressed their apprehension that once the Province of Quebec was included, as we all desire it to be, they would be left out in the cold. They certainly have been left out in terms of requirements for future meetings. I think that is very regrettable indeed.
I would like to ask the Prime Minister a supplementary question on the matter of spending authority and areas within the constitutional jurisdictional authority of the provinces. As the Prime Minister knows, the wording in the proposed agreement says that a province will be permitted to opt out of a new national program if its "own initiative or program is compatible with national objectives". This could have the constructive effect of institutionalizing what was done in Canada with the Quebec Pension Plan and the Canada Pension Plan. If so, it would be very good indeed. However, since another interpretation could be put on the wording that has been proposed to achieve this goal, is the Government of Canada open to specific amendments on the wording in this as well as other clauses?

Mr. Speaker, we have an agreement in principle which, as 1 have already indicated, in no way prevents the establishment of the kinds of national programs that are desired by my hon. friend and myself.
We are talking about future shared-cost programs in areas of exclusive provincial jurisdiction where the compensation takes place provided that the particular province itself erects a program that meets the national objectives that are set out originally. This is a fairly clear-cut statement of purpose that is consistent with strong federal presence and federal leadership at all times, but it is respectful of the rights of the provinces to have slight variations respecting their own requirements.
In responding to the question, Mr. Speaker, may I just take up a comment made by my hon. friend in regard to the aboriginal peoples having been left out in the cold because the Province of Quebec was included. I know the commitment of my hon. friend-
I didn't say that. I didn't say because Quebec was included.

That is what I took down. If it is in error, I apologize.
The point I want to make, something with which I do not think my hon. friend would disagree, is that the inclusion of the Province of Quebec is a significant guarantee of progress for the aboriginal peoples in terms of seeking justice for them at the constitutional table. The record of the Province of Quebec in regard to aboriginal rights is pretty exemplary visa-vis Canada. I believe that the presence of the Province of Quebec as a full partner around the First Ministers' Conference table called upon to deal with aboriginal questions will be a salutary and positive one and the aboriginal peoples should find encouragement in the progress we have made.

I entirely agree that the record of the Province of Quebec makes it very desirable that Quebec be there for this occasion. It would have been equally desirable to have institutionalized a requirement of an annual meeting until the aboriginal rights issue has been adequately dealt with.

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister did not indicate clearly the Government's attitude on its acceptance of proposed amendments. My supplementary question to the Prime Minister concerns the Yukon and Northwest Territories. It did not require unanimity when other provinces came into Confederation in the past, and the present amending formula does not require unanimity.
Many people in the North are planning to be able to come in one day on terms that are comparable to other provinces joining Confederation. Therefore, will the Prime Minister undertake to bring in an amendment to the clause pertinent to federal institutions that will at least leave the present amending formula in place, which is desirable to Canadians living in the Northwest Territories and Yukon?

Mr. Speaker, if my hon. friend consults the communique in regard to the principles agreed upon, I think he will see that there is an appropriate forum where these matters, particularly the one he just raised, can be properly addressed by First Ministers. It is proposed that we meet on a regular basis to deal with constitutional issues. Those issues pointed out were Senate reform, the fishery, and other matters that were felt appropriate, I believe, in point three.
It is not at all inconceivable that the matter raised by my hon. friend could well be considered at that point in time. It is important that this agenda be set out after all of the partners are back in the fold and that there is a unified constitutional document bringing the country together. I think we could then turn our minds to other matters in a helpful way. I thank my hon. friend for the suggestion.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT

speechtext: The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Hockin that Bill C-42, an Act respecting financial institutions and the deposit insurance system, be read the second time, and by unanimous consent, referred to the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate this afternoon has to do with Bill C-42 concerning financial institutions and, more particularly, the deposit insurance system.
Mr. Speaker, this is not the invention of the wheel nor the redevelopment of the nicest mouse trap, it is a long-awaited measure which I should imagine has been the subject of negotiations between the Government and the financial institutions for the past two years. It is one of a series of three Bills, we know that. The purpose of the first one-now under consideration, Bill C-42-is to merge financial institutions, those which are responsible for monitoring, the supervisory agencies for these institutions, namely the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance.
The powers of the new monitoring organization, to be called the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, and those of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will be strengthened. On that point we agree, Mr. Speaker.
Finally, the CDIC-Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation- will be allowed to raise its premium rates and authorized to borrow more from the Consolidated Revenue Fund.
The second Bill to follow, Mr. Speaker, is made up of two Bills that had already been introduced in this House and perhaps will be consolidated. They will give regulatory bodies the authority to issue cease and desist orders, and the Minister will have increased authority, the power to approve the takeover of major interests in financial institutions.
Finally, the third Bill-the third aspect of the matter-that should be tabled before summer, will have to deal with the powers of various types of institutions, the ownership system and the regulatory framework.
So, Mr. Speaker, we now have before us Bill C-42, an Act respecting financial institutions, and I would like to summarize for the House the impact of that legislation and put it into perspective.
Concerning regulatory bodies, Mr. Speaker, Bill C-42 proposes to amalgamate the Office of the Inspector General of Banks which, as we know, supervises chartered banks, and the Department of Insurance which supervises federally chartered loans and trust companies and insurance companies.
Financial Institutions
Those bodies are amalgamated into a single one called the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, the OSFI, and we support that move.
The CIDC, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, will remain independent, but closer coordination will be instituted between all regulatory bodies through the establishment of a new co-ordination committee.
Mr. Speaker, God knows that this House concerned itself with the problems of financial institutions for the past two and half years, since this Government came to power because, should I say in a sudden and dramatic way, major banking institutions were forced either to shut down, join others or even be taken over in order to survive, and in each or almost each of those cases the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation had to insure the costs either through payments to depositors or the advance of funds in order to secure or encourage foreign institutions-and I am thinking for instance of the Hongkong Bank in the matter of the Bank of British Columbia-to buy those institutions facing financial difficulty. As we know, Mr. Speaker, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation is an entity that insures loans by Canadians up to $60,000, and in many cases it is absolutely essential that we go on strengthening if not increasing the guarantee, in order that Canadian depositors enjoy greater security and the corporation may guarantee the deposits of Canadians, something we support.
Under Bill C-42, the new superintendent will have increased authority. It will become much easier for him to take the control of a financial institution facing difficulty. Such control in all cases will be for a period of seven days, or more if needed. Further, the superintendent may make decisions on behalf of the institution. Until now, as we know, he could not veto management decisions.
In the future, concerning the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, Bill C-42 proposes to increase from 1/10 of 1 per cent to 1/6 of 1 per cent the ceiling of rates for deposit insurance premiums paid by member institutions. Otherwise, Mr. Speaker, it used to be 1/30 of 1 per cent. We recently changed that to 1/10, and now we are going to increase it to 1/6 of 1 per cent. Currently, premiums are based on the 1/10 rate, as I said, and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) already announced that rate will be maintained for at least another year.
The CDIC's rates have already been increased in Bill C-86 which was passed in June of last year and I think that such a procedure is consistent with good management practices. In other words, when risks are greater, depositors must assuredly be protected, and since financial institutions have to replenish their coffers, the rates of contribution must be higher. They will therefore amount to one-sixth of 1 per cent in coming years.
Bill C-22 proposes to double the line of credit made available to the CDIC by the Government. This line of credit will increase from $1.5 billion to some $3 billion. The legislation will authorize the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to penalize the institutions whose practices are deemed risky or

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
somewhat unorthodox. It will make it possible for the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to decide whether or not to insure federal institutions, just as it does for provincial institutions. Now, federal institutions are automatically insured from the moment the regulatory agency issues their operating licence.
Finally, Bill C-42 will authorize the CDIC to cancel insurances to federal institutions, as it does already for provincial institutions, subject to the minister's authorization.
Mr. Speaker, the new committee responsible for co-ordinating the activities of monetary organizations, to which I referred a while ago, will be made up of the new Superintendent, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance, and the Chairman of the CDIC, meaning the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation.
The purpose of all of this, Mr. Speaker, is to organize better this major sector of our financial institutions by reinforcing if possible the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation on the one hand, and strengthening its terms of reference on the other.
Very briefly, Mr. Speaker, in order not to delay unduly the consideration of this Bill which, we hope, will not take too much time, I should like to remind the House that Bill C-42 is the result of events which occurred recently, or at least over the past two years. The House will remember the financial assistance which it had to give to the Canadian Commercial Bank in March 1985.
September 1985: Failures of the CCB and the Northland Bank. The House spent a long time dealing with this issue and even had to pass an emergency measure to bail out the banks and make sure that no investor in Canada would be penalized or suffer a major set-back.
December 1985: Compensation of all uninsured depositors of the Canadian Commercial Bank of Canada and the Northland Bank. The House will remember the billions which had to be paid to compensate those depositors.
End of 1985: The Mercantile Bank, whose financial foundations, at least according to the experts who were advising us, were quite sound, but which experienced cash flow problems because of the confidence crisis in the financial industry. The Mercantile Bank merged with the National Bank. Good initiative. Another banking institution saved.
End of 1985: The Morguard Bank, which again had sound financial foundations, but which experienced cash flow problems, had to merge with the Security Pacific Corporation, an American financial conglomerate. It was the first bank to pass under foreign control because of the lack of confidence in Canadian banks.
October 1985: The Continental Bank, with sound financial foundations, but again with cash flow problems, merged with Lloyds of London. That was the second bank to pass under foreign control.
In April 1986, approval from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) to the takeover of Canada Trust, a financial institution, by Imasco, a trade corporation, and we know the whole debate which surrounded the takeover of Canada Trust by Imasco. Could an institution, not necessarily a financial one,
take control over an entirely financial one? Need I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the debate was interesting, but lengthy.
In November 1986, not long ago, the Bank of British Columbia which, according to the experts, was practically bankrupt, merged with the Hongkong Bank and was the third to fall under foreign control. At that time, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation offered $200 million to the new buyers to encourage them and maybe sweeten the pill, telling them: "Once more, we, Canadians, must ask you to get us out of the mess." Mr. Speaker, in less than two years, three banks, three financial institutions went under foreign control.
I find that surprising, but what can I say? It has happened, and each time, the CDIC was involved, to help, facilitate or favour the deal. What will happen? Well, of course, as I said earlier in my remarks, the premiums will have to be raised, because there is a limit to giving billions of dollars to banks in difficulty and constantly reaching into general funds.
Therefore, the Government will raise the premium and in so doing, Mr. Speaker, will transfer its own deficit. It is responsible for its own deficit that will be transferred to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. About the deficit, Mr. Speaker, it has sky-rocketed in the last few years. It reached $1.1 billion on December 31, 1986, while on December 31, 1982, the CDIC recorded, I repeat, a $253 million surplus. So, in less that 15 years, we went from a surplus of $253 million to a deficit of $1.1 billion. That is the reason why we have to raise the premiums.
The main reason for the deficit is that the Government asked, or maybe ordered, the CDIC to take initiatives which were beyond its traditional role. I repeat, Mr. Speaker, that the corporation is only supposed to insure deposits up to a maximum of $60,000, but it was asked by the Government to participate actively in the operations to bail out troubled institutions.
For those who might have forgotten, 1 should mention that the CDIC provided $75 million to try and save the CCB, the Canadian Commercial Bank, in March of 1985. I repeat, $75 million in 1985. Then it gave $200 million to the Hongkong Bank so that the bank would buy the Bank of British Columbia in November, 1986. That money was used to refund uninsured depositors and even the shareholders got some of it. Not bad! Again, with the help of all depositors.
In February, 1987, $275 million was poured into the province of Alberta, your province, Mr. Speaker, to restructure the North West Trust Company. This is recent.
In each case, the decision was a political one and the costs should have been borne by the Treasury and the Government. We believe that they should have been added to the deficit. But they were not! The Government told the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation: You are going to bear the burden of those debts. It is therefore appropriate, Mr. Speaker, to say that the Government is shifting part of the burden of the deficit onto those institutions which are members of the CDIC and ultimately onto the customers of financial institutions.
May 4, 1987

I don't have to remind you, Mr. Speaker, that the Senate examined that matter and recommended in May 1986 that the costs of policy decisions should be borne by the Government.
Mr. Speaker, I do not want... I could elaborate at length on this matter, but I believe that the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will now be entitled to charge an additional contribution. It is a new right which carries important risks with it. Yet it is vital that the Corporation be entitled to charge those additional contributions to those who put at risk the rest of the institutions involved.
We would have preferred, Mr. Speaker, that the CDIC be allowed to establish separate insurance funds for banks and other financial institutions. The Government has not yet accepted that proposal, but we might decide to elaborate further on that point when we deal with the matter in committee. We therefore do not object to the amalgamation of the office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Department of Insurance. Indeed, we believe it is a worthwhile initiative and, as I said at the outset, I do not think this debate requires too much time or energy as we do agree, Mr. Speaker, on that initiative. It is our opinion that the second and third stages of this project will probably be of a more delicate and contentious nature, and we look forward of expressing our views on those when the Government decides to start that debate.
To summarize, Mr. Speaker, we welcome the additional powers granted to the reviewing agencies. Although it is not a very bold step in our opinion, it is still a first step. In our view, Bill C-42 is a step in the right direction, and we are proud to support this Government's initiative.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it has been some time since the time the Government first promised to bring forward this legislation and the day we first see it. I am sure most Canadians would find this subject that Parliament is debating extremely boring. In many ways the subject of financial institutions is the most boring you could conceivably talk about. It is full of quite complicated terms and concepts. Yet it surely is one of the most important subjects for Canadians and Parliament.
We are talking about the financial institutions where most Canadians invest their money, through savings accounts and other deposits. The fruits of their labour are kept in trust companies, banks and other institutions. We are also talking about insurance companies which carry policies on the average Canadian's life and home so that they can have some protection against the unforeseen. In many ways the well-being of the country is determined by these financial institutions because they can direct the flow of capital, which in many ways is the blood of the nation. It determines where economic activity will occur, how it occurs, in what kind of industry and so forth. Therefore, what we are speaking about this afternoon is really very important.
The Government that was elected in 1984 was very much committed to the notion of less Government and less regulation. It started its mandate with a desire to remove a lot of the regulations dealing with financial institutions. In fact, the
Minister introduced a Green Paper on the deregulation of financial institutions. But, lo and behold, the system was shown not to be over-regulated but under-regulated. As I am sure you will remember, a whole spate of pretty important financial institutions went belly up. Two chartered banks, the Canadian .Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank, both in Alberta, in essence ended up in receivership. In my Province of Saskatchewan Pioneer Trust went bankrupt. A whole slew of other trust companies and insurance companies have gone belly up. In some instances some depositors were hurt, those who had deposits of more than $60,000 in those institutions. In other cases, all the depositors were fully reimbursed despite the fact that deposit insurance covered them up to only $60,000. In fact, in the case of the CCB, millions of dollars were paid by the federal Treasury to other commercial banks because those banks had millions of dollars on short-term deposit at the CCB. That money was there because the CCB was paying a slightly higher interest rate. Those banks, while they knew the risk they were taking, decided to take the risk anyway because it gave them a little bit more of a return. However, it turned out they were not really taking a risk at all because the federal Government was quite prepared to pay them everything they would otherwise have lost.
We ended up in a strange situation. The Canadian Government borrows money from the banks in order to make up its deficit and then pays the bank interest. Here the Canadian Government had to borrow money from the banks at interest to pay back to the banks. Very strange. Somehow or other the banks never seem to lose. Certainly the taxpayers and the public of Canada have lost. Why did we have this situation where all these financial institutions, insurance companies and trust companies were going under? All at once everyone started asking: Where are the regulators? Where are the inspectors?
We thought we had institutions in place to prevent banks, insurance companies and trust companies from going belly up. Where were they? It appeared as though the regulatory agencies were indeed woefully inadequate in dealing with the crisis. You see, our regulators sort of assumed that our banks were controlled by a group of Methodist managers. It wasn't the fear of the Government or the regulators which forced them to be honourable gentlemen in banking, but the fear of God. If they tried to play hanky-panky with the books and other people's deposits, they would answer to God on the day of judgment.
We are now living in a new era. The smart boys on the street do not have the fear of God in them. They run circles around our regulators who do not have the street smarts which some of the financial whiz-kids have. They have found all sorts of loopholes in the regulations and hoodwinked the regulators in many instances.
May 4, 1987

It was really the fast boys who brought about the collapse of a fair number of our financial institutions such as Pioneer Trust, the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. In fact, when investigations were made into why these institutions went belly-up it was discovered that they were certainly not practising sound financial management. They were playing loose with other people's money, in some instances even to their own advantage. People have used other people's money for their own interest rather than in the interest of the depositors. It became obvious that some reform was needed. Today we have Bill C-42, with which I do not think too many in this House will have major disagreement. The only problem is that it is a little late. We wish this legislation had been brought forward somewhat earlier. Be that as it may, it is an important step in the right direction.
A new financial world is being created. I talked a moment ago about a time when bankers were Methodist ministers who were afraid of the day of judgment. That is no longer the case. We now have fast wheelers and dealers who play loose with other people's money. This is also an age of tremendous technological change. Money moves around the globe in a matter of minutes. In this day and age tremendously large and powerful national and multinational conglomerates have a tremendous amount of economic power because of the capital they control. They can blow away national interests, the rules of nations, and political jurisdictions because of the tremendous power which they have.
In some ways the Government is willing to play along with that. In some ways I understand why the Canadian Government believes it must play the game in order to attract capital into the country and that it must also go along with many of these changes. I am sympathetic with this. However, at the same time we must maintain a sense of Canadian control. We cannot allow a few large corporations to control the life-blood of the country. We cannot allow so much power in the hands of so few.
Sometimes I believe the Government is sending signals that it will allow that to occur as long as a few of the large and powerful conglomerates are so-called Canadian. I believe the Government is not honest with itself if it believes that simply because one or two of the owners of the conglomerate happen to have Canadian citizenship, it can be controlled by the nation state. In many ways their powers extend beyond the nation state within our borders.
The Government seems to be willing to go along with the collapse of the four pillars to allow one-stop financial shopping centres. In all the shopping malls across the country we will see one place where you can buy your insurance, make your deposits, buy bonds, and buy shares. As our colleague in the Liberal Party said in her address this morning, this change is not being driven by consumers demanding new services, it is being driven by the industry. I think she is so correct in that.
When the four pillars begin to collapse we will run into some problems. We increase the dangers of self-dealing and conflicts of interest. One part of the operation is making decisions
Financial Institutions
which affect and influence other parts of the operation. For example, will getting a mortgage on your home be dependent upon getting the insurance which that company is also selling? The potential of abuse increases. The modern technologies, the new type of ethics which exist in financial institutions and out on the street, and the creation of these new one-stop shopping centres all lead to a much greater potential for abuse of other people's moneys.
We need a new regime in terms of regulation. However, there is only so much the Government can regulate. The Government cannot send inspectors to sit beside every desk and watch every transaction. It would be insane for a government to try to do that. You cannot over-regulate the industry. You must hope to put in place some institutional form within which it is not in the interest of those to break the rules and regulations.
That is why we in this Party have been pushing very hard in committee and inside and outside of the House for wide ownership of financial institutions. That would help eliminate some of the causes of abuse. We hasten to add, however, that this is far from the total answer. Pioneer Trust in Regina is an example of a company which was quite widely held and yet experienced abuses in terms of self-dealing. Therefore, we are not saying that wide ownership will wipe out the possibility of self-dealing. We do say, however, that it reduces that possibility. It reduces the opportunity and motivation that some would have to use an institution for their self-interest rather than for the interest of the depositors. That is why we will continue to speak out for wider ownership.
I have another concern which is not directly related to Bill C-42 but is important, that is, the issue of regional financial institutions. Unfortunately, in the 1980s we have seen smaller regional financial institutions being severely weakened and going down the drain. In western Canada we have seen two banks in Alberta and the trust company in Saskatchewan go under. This is sad for us in western Canada as we attempt to get some control over our economic destiny. We need financial institutions in the west that are sensitive to our needs so we will be assured that there will be the necessary capital for the economic development of western Canada.
The unfortunate situation of two banks in Alberta and several trust companies in Alberta, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, as well as the disappearance of the Bank of British Columbia is a severe blow to western Canadians and our dream of economic development in the west. Hopefully, a better regulatory regime will ensure that smaller financial institutions will be more viable and we will no longer see the type of characters who were involved in the Canadian Commercial Bank and Pioneer Trust. They were partly responsible for the demise of those financial institutions, and we hope that better regulations will ensure that such a situation will not occur again.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
It is also true that those in the Maritimes are anxious to develop their own financial institutions that are sensitive to their needs and aspirations.
Therefore, we generally have no objection to Bill C-42 and will support it. There will be an opportunity to examine it more closely in committee where I expect the Government will be open to suggestions for amendments to this legislation by the finance committee. When the Government realized that the Green Paper would not be accepted, it held consultations and sought advice. I believe it is willing to accept some amendments that might improve the Bill and allow for stronger financial institutions in this country.
