subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I intend to speak at second reading of Bill C-42. I did not intend to get involved in the type of debate raised by my colleague, the Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). However, I think I will take a few minutes to put his remarks in context.
The Bill we are discussing now was tabled for first reading on March 3, 1987. It is not my fault if the Government House Leader did not ask the Speaker to call second reading of the Bill before today. The opposition Parties are not responsible for that decision, it is the Government's decision.
If the Member for Mississauga South is telling us that it is an urgent matter, I must remind him that the Green Paper was tabled in April, 1985. This is now May 4, 1987 and this is the first day of debate. I do not know how we could be accused of delaying this piece of legislation. The type of remark just made by my colleague may bring us to consider in more detail this legislation because I wonder why the Hon. Member wants us to adopt the legislation so urgently. I suppose I can understand that, but at least the Government could give us a few hours. We have not even spent a day on this Bill. I am the third speaker on my side to address this legislation.
May 4, 1987

Mr. Speaker, as was said earlier, this is an important piece of legislation, and its purpose is to modify the supervisory agencies responsible for the proper functioning of our financial institutions. How does this Bill propose to achieve this objective? First of all, by modifying the structure of the regulatory agencies.
I believe the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn) made a slight mistake a while ago when he said that the Bill was a direct response to the recommendations in the report of the Standing Committee of the House of Commons on Finance and Economic Affairs. 1 may remind the Hon. Member that the Committee's report was not unanimous, since a minority report was filed by Opposition Members.
Furthermore, in its proposal to restructure the regulatory agency, Bill C-42 did not follow the recommendation to which the Chairman of the House of Commons Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs was alluding. In the Bill, the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the office of the Superintendent of the Department of Insurance would be merged, but not the office of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, which was supposed to be part of the megaagency proposed by the majority of the Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs.
I recall saying at the time that the proposition made by the Conservative majority of the House Standing Committee on Finance and Economic Affairs was an elephant whose administration would be very cumbersome indeed. I am glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has heeded the remarks of the Official Opposition and drawn a clear line to separate the operations of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation, but to regroup under one organization both the Office of the Inspector General of Banks and the Bureau of the Superintendent of Insurance of Canada which has always monitored federal institutions, what we call the federally-chartered trust companies.
Therefore the purpose of this measure is to restructure this control organization very much along the lines recommended by the Liberal Party. Second, this organization will have more powers and for all practical purposes the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, should he see fit and after consulting his council colleagues, will be able to take over the administartion of a financial institution for seven days and impose his instructions and decisions to the institution for reasons which the superintendent would have deemed significant enough to impose the necessary changes and use his right of veto. I think this will improve the controlling organization and I am pleased this has been included.
The second aspect of the Bill on which I will have a few comments, Mr. Speaker, is the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. Hon. Members will recall thai amendments were made to that legislation, when this Conservative Government decided to increase from 1/30 to 1/10 of 1 per cent the level of premiums paid by financial institutions on insurable deposits.
Financial Institutions
We now see that this Government, not satisfied with trebling the cost of insurance deposits, chose to increase it once more by raising the rate from 1/10 to 1/6 of 1 per cent. The Government however will keep that flexibility to decide, probably by order in council, what he will do with the premium increase.
The Minister indicated, I think last week in a press release, his intention to maintain premiums at the current level. But how long will it remain there? It will be left entirely to the Minister to increase the rate from 1/10 of 1 per cent to 1/6 of 1 per cent. To my mind, this is a tax that will in effect be determined by order in council, and I would have preferred that when that move is made, it could be debated in the House of Commons and the parties involved had a public opportunity to be heard, and Members in this House were informed of the reasons why the Government chose once more to increase that indirect tax which in the long run will be borne by consumers, because certainly financial institutions will pass the cost on to consumers by changing either the cost of financial services or interest rates.
The other purpose of this Bill, Mr. Speaker, is to increase the credit margin of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to $3 billion. This will double its credit margin, and in this case also, I think that considerable power will be given to the Minister under this amendment to the Act. Bill C-42, the legislation we are dealing with, will make it possible for the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to penalize the institutions whose practices are deemed risky or unorthodox. It will also allow the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to decide whether or not to insure federal institutions, just as it does already for provincial institutions.
Mr. Speaker, it will make it possible for the Corporation to cancel the insurance of federal financial institutions, subject to the Minister's authorization.
Mr. Speaker, those three powers which will be given to the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation will have indirectly the result which the Govermment did not want to obtain directly, namely to create different pools for different types of corporations. Mr. Speaker, if, with the Minister's authorization, the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation imposes a surcharge to a financial institution, although we are assured that the information will not be released to the press, information travels so fast nowadays that when the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation makes such a decision, I am afraid that within a few months or weeks, if not days, the public will learn about it and confidence in the financial institution will be jeopardized, which would mean that the Minister would be signing the death warrant of this financial institution, because to develop, a financial institution requires the confidence of its depositors. We know what happened with the Northland Bank and the Canadian Commercial Bank. When the public became aware of their financial difficulties, depositors withdrew their money. Not only those two banks were directly affected but two other financial institutions that were in a good position in terms of the quality of their assets were also indirectly affected

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
and had cash flow problems beyond their control. Those problems, for all practical purposes, forced the Mercantile and Continental Banks to merge with other financial institutions and to reduce competition in that area. Therefore, I have strong reservations as regards the ability of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation to collect premium surcharges, in other words to indirectly create separate pools for financial institutions, without running the risk of destroying those institutions.
Finally, in order to ensure co-ordination between the new organization and the Deposit Insurance Corporation, the Minister decided to create a co-ordination committee consisting of the new Superintendant of Financial Institutions, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Deputy Minister of Finance and the Chairman of the Board of the Canada Deposit Insurance Corporation. That is a good proposal, Mr. Speaker. In doing that, we institutionalize through legislation a Committee that was anyway probably meeting on an emergency basis. But the establishment of that co-ordination committee and its obligation to sit as well as the fact that the committee members will not be able to be replaced by their assistants will ensure, through consultation between those different groups, namely the Superintendant of Financial Institutions, the new Superintendant, the Governor of the Bank of Canada, the Department of Finance and the Chairman of the CDIC, an exchange of financial information that will facilitate, I think, the good management and control of financial institutions.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member who spoke previously outlined the importance and the urgency of Bill C-42 and we obviously believe that it is important to change as well as to strenghten controls, given the disastrous experience Canada has had over the last couple of years. First, there was the Canadian Commercial Bank bankruptcy, then that of the Northland Bank. Then there were other financially troubled institutions, one of which merged with Security Pacific Corporation. There was also the case of the Continental Bank which merged with an institution called Floyds Bank and, of course, the merger of the Bank of British Columbia with the Hongkong Bank. So many downfalls are due in large part of course, I believe, and I said so at the time, to a lack of foresight on the part of a Government whose main concern it was to solve a serious problem in such a way as to fend off any bad news which might have clouded the economic conference which had been presided by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mul-roney). But we now see what consequences such a hasty and ill advised decision has had on several financial institutions and not only on the Canadian Commercial Bank.
Mr. Speaker, I would also like to say that this bill is not- that it would have been easier to deal with it if we had known how the Government intends to structure other financial institutions, how it intends to deal with the problem of relationships between insurance companies and trusts, banks and real estate companies. It would then have been easier for us to determine whether this new legislation, Bill C-42, is
geared to deal effectively with the new structures and the new implications they will have for the financial sector as a whole.
I have already had the opportunity to voice my concerns publicly with regard to the leeway which our brokerage firms enjoy at present. As of June 30, they are possible candidates for the big bang, as it has been termed in England at the time of deregulation. And this leeway, this possibility of taking over Canadian investment dealers will be open not only to Canadian institutions but to foreign firms as well. And I understand banks have some concerns about it, and the legislation as we understand it, according to the paper tabled by the Hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), could lead us into a strange situation where a Canadian bank might buy a brokerage firm and have to close down its brokerage operations in the United States, since the U.S. regulations do not allow a brokerage firm to be the property of a bank such as the Royal Bank, the Bank of Commerce or the Savings Bank, in other words, any bank which buys a brokerage firm.
Thus, there would be no reciprocity in the operations between Canada and the United States.
Secondly, Mr. Speaker, insofar as a Canadian bank would buy a brokerage firm, as I just mentioned, with things standing as they are, it would have to close down this broker's operations in the United States, whereas if a U.S. company buys 100 per cent of this same Canadian brokerage firm, it could operate in Canada and in the United States without any problem whatsoever in terms of legislation and regulations. I feel we have acted very quickly. Once again, the Government has decided to give this possibility to the Americans, whereas no reciprocity exists for Canadians, and all this is done, it seems to me, outside the context of our free trade discussions with the United States.
Mr. Speaker, the reason I have concerns on the matter of our brokerage firms is that brokers act as advisors for their clients, and because they are 100 per cent owned by a bank or a trust company and those banks and trust companies or those insurance companies will apparently have the ability to get into the commercial loans area, We would find ourselves in a situation where a broker-in dealing with an industrialist who wants to issue bonds to repay his medium-term loans to a bank-would be in a bind, in terms of conflict of interests or loyalties between his shareholder, from whom the loan is to be bought, and the issuer who is looking for the best possible terms to refinance his business.
I feel that the potential for conflict of interests is there, and we should look at that in a very particular and special way before we abolish the independence of our brokers.
Others said that if we did not do that, especially as regards the financial industry, if we do not do that, we are preventing our Canadian institutions from playing a role internationally. Yes, well! It is all very well to say that, but as far as I am concerned I find it hard to believe that once the Solomon Brothers, the Merrill Lynches, the Shearson Lehmans and the
May 4, 1987

other big American firms have bought our Dominion Securities and our other brokerage firms, those big American firms who are already established internationally, be it in New York, London, Tokyo or in other European countries, in Paris, that those big international corporations .. . And the same would apply if Nomura bought one of those firms. Certainly those large multinational corporations, I would be very much surprised if they transferred their decision centres from New York or Tokyo or London or Germany to Toronto or Montreal or Vancouver or any other Canadian city to perform the international financing activities involved.
For those reasons, Mr. Speaker, I reserve my final judgment until I see the follow-up on Bill C-42. But I want to express my concerns right now, because it is my feeling that they are destroying a financial system that has served Canadians well and that could lead to difficulties as regards the role of Canadian companies in catering to the financial needs of our businesses and institutions.
They say this kind of deregulation, that Bill C-42 that is part of a three-pronged legislative effort, the two other parts of which are not yet known, will facilitate company integration. My colleague earlier referred to shopping centres as far as financial institutions are concerned. I can visualize that in some cases. I was part of a financial group before coming to this House. We had goals that of course were connected with our operations of that time. But I am asking myself serious questions: Do we do know of anyone in today's world, a Canadian consumer, who one morning rises and tells himself: Today 1 am doing my financial shopping? And that someone goes to the shopping centre, and buys his insurance, his shares, his bonds, and make his deposits? That is not the way things operate in the financial world. You do not shop for financial services the way you shop for groceries. A degree of caution is in order. Furthermore, 1 might add that if we want to develop this kind of financial trading centre, my biggest concern is that the great winner, the institutions it will benefit the most are the major financial institutions, that is to say, the major banks that already enjoy a wide network at every street corner in each of our large cities and towns. It will be awfully hard for other institutions to compete, whether they are life insurance or general insurance companies, because the banks have their own network, and insurance agents do not necessarily have the ability to give the expected financial services. Doing away with the so-called four pillars might have unexpected results, concerning first of all the brokers but also the insurance companies and the banks.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal with the trust companies-
As you are indicating that my time is up, I shall have no time for those final remarks. I suppose that when we study other pieces of legislation, I shall have the opportunity to explain the reasons of my concerns regarding the potential conflicts of interests between trust operations, financial operations in general, insurance, and banking.
Financial Institutions

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I ask my Liberal colleague if he would comment with respect to the question of ownership guidelines within the banking sector. Does he think a Bill such as this would not have provided a regulatory environment which was much more effective in protecting consumers and achieving economic policy goals if it had a much stricter limitation on the share of equity ownership possible within given financial institutions?

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first, I would have preferred to study Bill C-42 along with the other legislation. It would have been easier to evaluate. Perhaps the supervision and control in this legislation is enough, but I do not know what the other legislation will provide.
As far as ownership is concerned, my personal view is that it depends on the size of the company or the financial institution. This is why I agreed in general terms with the proposal made by the finance committee concerning what should be taken into account for ownership. While our views differ on whether for example 100 per cent ownership should be for $10 billion or $15 billion worth of assets, that is a point of view I am prepared to discuss. Generally speaking, the approach we suggested is, I believe, appropriate.
If we abolish completely the four pillars and open up the possibility of a bank owning an insurance company or a trust company or vice versa, I would suggest very strongly that there be no interconnection between financial institutions and industrial organizations. I have nothing against a big financial institution getting bigger, but I have a lot of concern even if only 15 per cent or 30 per cent of such an institution is owned by one party. When the rest of the shares are spread out in the public, it does not take 51 per cent to control a board of directors. I would prefer to see a complete distinction between financial institutions and industrial organizations, and we said so in our minority report which was tabled after the report from the finance committee was tabled.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, what perspective would my colleague put on the level of foreign ownership of a banking or near banking institution that might be permitted? Is this something he would be prepared to maintain within narrow limits, or would a relaxation of those rules be acceptable to him?

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I said publicly that I accepted the fact that foreign financial institutions can come to Canada. I have nothing against Schedule B foreign banks. On the contrary, it creates more competition and forces Canadian financial institutions to evolve, to become more competitive and to become more creative. I think it has been a positive step and I have nothing against it. However, if we are to suggest that large banks should be open to foreign sales, we should keep a limitation on total ownership. Up until now there has been a maximum, and I think it should be kept. I have no objection to foreign ownership of smaller financial institutions.

May 4, 1987
Financial Institutions
When it comes to investment dealers, I think it is a different game altogether. We should try to keep Canadian control over these institutions and certainly not open the country up as it will be open after June 30. If a foreign organization can buy 50 per cent of a Canadian investment dealer, the foreign company will effectively control the organization and after June 30, 1988, the company will probably buy out the rest of the shares. That is something that has preoccupied me a lot, and I would strongly suggest that the Government look at this possibility before June 30 and give the House a chance to debate it because there is the possibility that we may kill a Canadian financial industry we took so many years to build.

subtopic: FINANCIAL INSTITUTIONS AND DEPOSIT INSURANCE SYSTEM AMENDMENT ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to express my pleasure in being able to take part in this debate. First I would like to congratulate the Hon. Member for Mississauga South (Mr. Blenkarn). I recall that when the first proposals for reform in financial institutions were brought before the House, a great many of us had serious doubts about exactly what was being proposed. I believe the Hon. Member has succeeded in putting across a powerful point of view which led to significant changes in the approach taken by the Government, and I congratulate him for that. That does not, of course, mean that I now agree with the Bill which is before us in its entirety, but I think that the personal achievement of the Hon. Member deserves to be recognized.
One of the questions the Hon. Member himself raised not too long ago was why there was an interest in speaking in this debate and putting forth the considerations and concerns of our constituents. Frankly, I must say that the last two and a half years have seen the greatest shake-up in confidence in the Canadian banking sector the country has experienced since the 1920s and the continent has experienced since the 1930s. It is a shake-up which we on this side of the House have found unfortunate and especially devastating because of the nature of the bail-outs of the banks which got themselves into trouble.
However, it is important at this stage in the debate that people across the country and those of us in the House of Commons keep very much in mind what one newspaper has called the "chronicle of carelessness and collapse" which affected the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank. Certainly it is for that reason that we have before us a Bill which is supposed to establish the solution. Frankly, I am not overly convinced that the solution has been achieved.
This Bill will create a super-bureaucracy. It will tie that super-bureaucracy to a series of inputs from important parts of the financial community. However, I cannot see within it guarantees that give Canadians a greater sense of security in respect of the future of their banking system.
So far we have been fortunate. Our banking system has had two collapses, which of course had not occurred since 1923 when the Home Bank collapsed. These two collapses are combined with the collapses of a number of trust and loan companies. There is a potential for a much more serious crisis in the future banking system because of the tremendous openness which the banking system showed itself to have in
respect of foreign loans to the Third World. A great many of those loans at this stage are highly questionable.
I could take Hon. Members through at least six significant foreign debtors in the Third World which have, within the last year, very significantly changed their approach to repayment of their foreign debts. We could talk of Peru. We could talk of Equador. We could talk of the most recent country which has joined in this protest, namely Zambia.
We must recognize that there is before us something which has been unprecedented in the Canadian banking history. There is a threat to the stability of these banks because of the Third World debt crisis and the incapacity of international institutions such as the IMF to solve the debt crisis of the Third World. The consequent reality is that at least a significant number of our large banks are susceptible to the failure of certain Third World countries to pay back interest and to maintain loans which are considered to be performing loans. That capacity is limited increasingly in the Third World and, as a consequence, our banks feel the chill winds of challenge.
All of us would like to believe that the regulatory agency to be created here would somehow be able to solve the problem. Frankly I do not think that the problem is even touched by the creation of this kind of super-bureaucracy. Therefore, if one had a sense that the Government had some kind of broader strategy regarding the future of our financial institutions, it would be very much easier for those of us on this side of the House to rush through a Bill like this one, with the kind of celerity suggested by the Hon. Member for Mississauga South.
In point of fact, however, that situation does not exist. There are problems with our banking system which have been demonstrated by two catastrophic failures, by very significant expenditure of public funds to bail out the creditors of those two banks, and by the continuing debt crisis in the Third World, which is very much a backdrop threatening our existing banks.
In addition to a lack of strategy in respect of the Third World crisis, there is a lack of strategy in the Government, which I find acceptable, anyway, on the question of ownership in banking. I understand that part of the reason for that lack of strategy is that there is a negotiation taking place with the United States which may open entirely the country to foreign banks from the United States to operate here as if Canada were simply another state of the union. In those circumstances it is extremely difficult for policy makers to shape strategy and to set out what should be future ownership levels within the Canadian banking sector.
Nevertheless, a great deal could be achieved by being quite strict at this stage by putting into effect and carrying forward the 10 per cent limitation on foreign ownership of our large-scale banks. If we were to do that, it would give a great deal more credibility to the capacity of the institution which the Bill aims to create to be able to regulate and control the banking system within the country.
May 4, 1987

If we look down the road five years from now and see before us a tremendous proliferation of all kinds of U.S. banks right across Canada, a super-bureaucracy will be created as this Bill attempts to do. That super-bureaucracy will become absolutely bogged down in the details of simply trying to keep up with the hundreds of important large-scale banks which will be operating within Canada. That is a very serious gap in the legislation before us at the moment.
It is important that there be a counter vision, if you like, to the very narrow vision which essentially sees the continuation of the status quo, a status quo which will have a slightly larger, more powerful bureaucracy in control of it, which is what this legislation really represents. Banking is very much at the heart of economic policy and economic development for any country. Yet I do not see within this legislation, I do not see within the thinking of the Government in so far as one can assess it, any creative, imaginative new approaches to making use of the banking system in Canada as a tool for profound economic development which can reshape the country and give much more fairness to all the different parts of our community and to all the different elements within our society.
There has to be a much wider perspective brought to bear on the question of banking than is present in the Bill before us at this stage. I think of the development banking which exists in the Netherlands, a development banking system which was established by the Government there. subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise today to speak on the matter of legislation which, in part, suggests that the Government consider a royal commission to look into organized crime. Her motion also suggests that we should study the proceeds of organized crime. It is that aspect of the motion which I would like to address today because it is apparent that Canada is presently deficient in its ability to battle the scourge of organized crime by confiscating the fruits of crime.
It is apparent that criminals here are able to establish an opulent life-style through the profits from illegal activity and then laugh at the judicial system if caught. This exists because, once apprehended and sentenced, their financial empire continues unaffected by the judicial process. They serve their
Organized Crime
sentences only to be released to enjoy the benefit of their criminality which remains intact and untouched.
This is unfortunate on two counts. First, it brings the entire administration of justice into disrepute and, second, recognizes that traditional methods of sentencing based on deterrence, both specific and general, are woefully inadequate to deal with the modern phenomena of organized crime.
Police officers with experience in the area of organized crime will advise you of the frustration they feel when they have spent months or years on an investigation which has resulted in a substantial sentence handed down by the court. They know that they and society are laughed at when the criminal is released from the penitentiary to enjoy even increased wealth because of the wise investment of his or her criminal profits. There is a new slogan today: Crime definitely pays.
We should not fool ourselves into believing that this type of activity is limited to the drug trade. Its connections in the area of child pornography, prostitution and illegal gambling are well documented. Extortion and murder are merely the marketing skills of drug traffickers. Any consistent attack on this problem requires legislation against drug profits and other related criminal activity.
Today's modern criminal organization has become a "full service" institution. Anything from insurance fraud to arson is available for a price. It is at that monetary level that legislative initiative must be directed. It is the life-blood of the criminal enterprise. If it is cut off, the body that feeds it will die.
There is another aspect of this problem which bears mentioning as well. It is now becoming apparent that these criminal organizations have an impact that is not limited to police and health concerns. There is an economic and political element which is most disturbing. I refer to the recent newspaper articles which detailed the description of such organizations as the Medellin cartel in Colombia. This group is not only the source of much of the drug trade that is generated in the South American country of Colombia, but it also appears that this group is powerful enough to affect the stability and, therefore, the independence of that democracy. It lives by terror and assassination as a means of retaliation for any arrests of its members.
The Government and the judiciary of Colombia have been victims of these attacks, and it is obvious that this group is powerful enough to be a threat to the very continued existence of the Colombian state. All this terror is financed by the cocaine trade, 80 per cent of which comes from North America. Canada, along with other western nations, is financing the destruction of this democracy by enabling domestic criminal organizations to enjoy and enlarge their financial empires.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion presented by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Mrs. Nicholson) which proposes appointing a royal commission of Inquiry on organized crime in Canada is, I think, at least as far as the intent of the motion is concerned, based on the assumption that organized crime exists in Canada and this despite that memorable cliche that crime does not pay. It has been said time and time again, I learned it when I was in school, and I have even heard it on television as a slogan: crime does not pay. Mr. Speaker, if crime did not pay, there would be no crime. When our policemen tell us proudly that 62 per cent or 50 per cent or 45 per cent of the crimes committed in
this country are solved, there are still 50 per cent that are not, and in many cases they have paid very well indeed. The concept that crime does not pay just does not wash, Mr. Speaker.
Of course, when you get caught, it is another story. In any event, what the Hon. Member wanted to point out is that it is absolutely necessary to fight organized crime. Mr. Speaker, it would be nice if the Hon. Member had been here today to defend her Bill, because the Liberal benches are not exactly crowded today. For the last 15 minutes I have not seen a soul. However, Mr. Speaker, the underworld exists-

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext: I had hoped the Hon. Member would not mention the attendance of anyone in or out of the Chamber. They may be behind the curtain or watching the Hon. Member on television.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, your attitude to the Opposition is most charitable.
Mr. Speaker, there is an underworld in Canada. There are people who, as we say in Quebec, would kill their mother to go to the orphan's dance. There are people who will stop at nothing. The end justifies the means, however sordid. The concept of gain, of venality is so ingrained that they stop at nothing to get what they want. They will stop at nothing to organize crime, to make it into a regular system, to institutionalize it. Actually, Mr. Speaker, the underworld, however somber and sordid, has become part of our world as well. Mr. Speaker, many people cannot help admiring the way certain criminals or gangsters pull off a particularly successful coup.
Who could resist making a good bargain at a certain point, Mr. Speaker, buying the little gold watch at an absolutely unbeatable price? Of course, when it has been stolen, there is a problem, but we don't even question that.
This is a good time of the year to talk about income tax. Well, Mr. Speaker, we all try to cheat the income tax system a little now and then. Organized crime exists because the seed of crime is present in all of us.
My colleague also asks for a Royal Commission on organized crime in Canada. Organized crime is organized not only in Canada, but in the United States, in South America, and, why not, in Iran, in Thailand, just about everywhere? This Commission should work in every direction, as brilliantly demonstrated by CECO, the Quebec Commission on Organized crime, by catching a few leaders or a few gangs! Organized crime has its roots a bit everywhere in the world. Therefore, what we need is not a Royal Commission on organized crime in Canada but maybe an international commission of inquiry, but at what cost?
May 4, 1987

Furthermore, if we want to know the way organized crime operates, how it works, I think it has been known for a long time to our policemen. I think it is not very useful to explain all the tricks those people use to get what they want. 1 think the problem comes mainly from our Criminal Code, Mr. Speaker.
We live in a society which has a lot of respect for the individual. We have our Charter of Rights. We talk about human rights, but our system that shows enormous respect for those rights treats with the greatest care men and women who are known criminals, underworld figures who come to court dressed up to the nines, who demand the best consideration and have committed a countless and unbelievable number of crimes very difficult to prove. That is a problem. Our policemen have to get almost ironclad evidence confirmed by eyewitnesses. It is extremely difficult to get criminals convicted. Policemen are at their wits' end. They have thick records on some people whose guilt is impossible to prove in court. It is extremely difficult to get a conviction. And our judicial system that is undoubtedly too generous, too permissive, allows those individuals to go scot-free all too easily. Often our whole parole system comes into play, and so on and so forth. Those underworld leaders keep at their job, their line of work. Imagine, we call that a line of work! We say: They work in their field. As you see, it is institutionalized indeed.
Personally, Mr. Speaker, despite my colleague's concerns, I feel the case has been made, it would be a waste of money. What would such a commission cost? Fifteen million dollars? Twenty million dollars? What use would it have? Drafting beautiful and thick reports only to shelve them. For a while, of course, the exercise could upset the underworld and a few heads could roll with additional investigators and endless prosecutions.
I think it would be better for this money to assist our police which, generally speaking, do an excellent work. I wish to commend the Surete du Quebec, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police well known for their good name. With this money they could set up more specialized teams, increase their communications network, strenghten their international relations and communications, and equip themselves with state of the art tools in an effort to finally capture these underworld kingpins and dismantle organized crime.
Mr. Speaker, we should all work together towards amending our Criminal Code, making it more relevant and seeing that the work of our policemen bring these individuals the sentences they deserve.
I as well as police officers often wonder, Mr. Speaker, about the value of our system which like an huge net, lets bigger fish go through all the time and in greater number. It seems that only the small fish get caught. The sharks are the ones that escape, Mr. Speaker. Such is our system. We compare justice to a huge net where all the fish get trapped but for fear of condemning an innocent we release a few. What I find interesting is the fact that the big sharks manage to go through this net and the small fish, the little guy, the diminutive get caught easily.
Organized Crime
I agree with my colleague that the appropriation of the proceeds of organized crime could help us effectively and actively fight this criminal element of our society by providing us the necessary financial and manpower resources to stand up to it in the most direct way.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, that is a tough act to follow, but I will try. I am pleased to participate in the debate on the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) that a royal commission be established to investigate organized crime in Canada.
The Hon. Member for Trinity has set out a number of suggested terms of reference for this royal commission into organized crime, and I want to take this opportunity to say a few words about the extent to which we as a society should be examining our system of justice to ensure that, in fact, it reflects the principles of equity and fairness and those principles which should be at the heart of an effective system of justice so that it is not one that primarily targets those who are most vulnerable and weak in our society.
Let me begin by quoting from Jessica Mitford, a well-known author who wrote the following in 1973 in a book entitled Kind and Unusual Punishment:
Envision, if you can, a prison system populated primarily by the white and well-to-do, convicted of crimes that are peculiar to the affluent: price-fixing, product adulteration, industrial pollution, criminal neglect of industrial safety standards-(knowingly selling unsafe automobiles) violation of the minimum wage laws. That this notion seems like the wildest flight of fancy is already a commentary on the class character of the prison system.
It is axiomatic that as long as privileges of class and colour prevail in a society, this state of affairs will be reflected in its prisons and will determine who coerces whom.
I think those words are accurate and well founded just as were the words of the Chief of Police in suburban Saanich, British Columbia, John Post. He said, and I quote:
You see very few privileged people in jail,... The old saying that there is a law for the rich and a law for poor is alive and well.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) talked about the big fish and the little fish and the fact that the big fish are very seldom caught by the net. I think on that point, if not on all of the points he made, I am in agreement. I think there are many examples of this.
I recently had the honour of being invited to speak as a graduation speaker at the Matsqui Institution campus of Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. Simon Fraser offers a very excellent program on post-secondary education. As I looked around at that captive audience, as it were, I asked myself how many of those prisoners were there because they had broken Canada's laws with respect to the environment, because they had polluted our waters or poisoned our lakes and streams. How many of those prisoners were there as a result of corporate negligence? How many of them were there as corporate executives who, through their negligence, took actions which resulted in the death or serious injury to workers?

May 4, 1987
Organized Crime
We know that some 700 people in 1984 died in the workplace. So when we talk about organized crime and white-collar crime, I think it is important that we not lose sight of how we as a society define crime. I suspect that not many of the prisoners in that particular institution, or in any other institution in Canada, were responsible for manufacturing unsafe or hazardous products. However, corporate executives, in their desire for profit, manufactured flammable children's night-gowns and automobile executives manufactured automobiles they knew were dangerous and a risk to the safety of society.
Finally, when we talk about organized crime and white-collar crime, I think it is important to note as well that there has been quite a significant increase in the level of this type of crime. As long ago as 1980, it was revealed that the level of white-collar crime in Canada was increasing dramatically. Over $1 billion a year, for example, was lost in insurance fraud alone. In 1972, the RCMP had about 2,500 active files on white-collar offences. At the end of 1978, some six years later, there were in excess of 10,000 files. So when we talk about crime and an increase in the level of crime in our society, we must not lose sight of white-collar crime as well and the extent to which our society is still not prepared to tackle that as a serious problem.
There are many examples of this crime, whether it be security-related fraud, embezzlement, pilferage, insurance fraud, computer assisted crime, commercial counterfeiting of parts or, indeed, of money, arson and a whole range of similar crimes. The offence of pollution is a very serious one, yet our society still does not take it seriously enough. It is ironic that back in 1307 the penalty in England for violating air pollution standards was capital punishment. In 1986 the maximum fine a Canadian court could impose for an offence under the Federal Fisheries Act was $50,000. I have not heard the Hon. Member for Peterborough (Mr. Domm) suggest that we string up corporate executives who are responsible for pollution, for destroying our environment or responsible, through negligence, for the death of workers. No, the Hon. Member is silent on that particular matter.
What about the corporations which are responsible for selling hazardous and unsafe goods? Canada Packers in 1981 pleaded guilty to selling a contaminated drug which was potentially lethal for pregnant women. Did those corporate executives who were responsible go to jail? Of course not. They were fined the maximum fine under the Food and Drugs Act of $5,000. They were fined $5,000 for selling contaminated drugs which were potentially fatal for pregnant women.
Our society has to re-examine the way in which we define crime. We have to examine as well those who are in fact prosecuted for crimes. My colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), has put forward a motion with respect to the particular role of organized crime. She has focused on the extent of the involvement of organized crime in
a number of areas, including drugs, loan sharking and other illegal activities.
I see my colleague the Hon. Member for Megantic- Compton-Stanstead (Mr. Gerin) is in the House. I think it is interesting to note that he and some of his colleagues from the Province of Quebec have urged the Government to take action with respect to corporate donations to political Parties in order to eliminate the risk that this may lead to corruption, illegality and wrongdoing, and I congratulate the Hon. Member for bringing forward this proposal. I think it is an excellent one and one we should be looking at it in the context of our discussions on white-collar crime.
Surely, as well, we have to ask ourselves how it is that organized crime makes these massive profits. We know that its profit is something in the order of $10 billion a year and of that $10 billion, drugs are the big money makers at more than $9 billion a year. Surely we should ask ourselves whether our approach to drugs in Canada is one which ultimately results in incredible profits for a small number of people at the highest possible level, and if we should not take another look at our drug laws. Are they effectively serving our community or just serving the interests of a very small number involved in organized crime?
Similarly, organized crime is involved in other activities, including prostitution, pornography, theft, counterfeiting and fraud. As a result of the tabling of recent pornography provisions in this House, I suspect we may even see a greater role for organized crime. This Government has failed miserably to make that fundamental distinction between erotica and pornography which is so essential. In not doing so, the Government will drive it underground right into the hands of organized crime.
I suggest that we as a society must re-examine our priorities with respect to criminal law and recognize that there must not be any longer one system of law for the rich and the powerful and another quite different system of law for those who are poor and powerless.
Recently, three corporate officials in Illinois were convicted of murder as a result of the intentional causing of the cyanide poisoning deaths of employees through unsafe work practices. The corporate boardroom surely cannot be exempt from the reach of criminal law, and I would hope that any royal commission which examines the role of organized crime in our society would look very carefully as well at the whole question of white-collar crime during the course of that much needed examination.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am always interested in initiatives proposed by my colleagues here in the House of Commons about criminal matters. I am particularly supportive of the motion which is before us today moved by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson), which deals with a subject of considerable importance in major urban centres as well as in all parts of Canada. It has to do with the fact and presence of organized crime.
May 4, 1987

Organized crime is not a new phenomenon by any stretch of the imagination. However, occasionally, its existence is denied in Canada, and then usually within weeks of such denial by someone in authority there is some concrete evidence of it. I believe that organized crime is present in Canada. It is simply the existence of even as small a group as two or more individuals consorting together on a continuing basis to participate in illegal activity either directly or indirectly for gain.
To my way of thinking these are illegal activities which are not logically or necessarily related to each other. They are different types of activities such as those involving drugs and prostitution, the fencing of property, loan sharking and the importation and distribution of pornographic material. I have that type of activity in mind when I think of organized crime. I know that such activity occurs in our country.
I wish to focus on one particular part of the mandate proposed for the establishment of a royal commission to investigate organized crime, since it is quite broad. It includes an examination of the extent to which organized crime is present and active in Canada, particularly in such activities as drug trafficking and loan sharking; the extent to which organized crime is connected to the institutions of Canadian society; action taken by the Governments of other countries to investigate and curtail organized crime activity; legislation to enable the Government to identify and appropriate the proceeds of organized crime; effective and appropriate punishment in instances of organized crime murder conspiracy; and possible guidelines for enforcement agencies in dealing with witnesses against organized crime.
You might find it interesting, Mr. Speaker, if I offer a couple of my own reflections on the subject of organized crime in Canada. It is a business. One of the interesting things that is found in organized crime in Canada is that it tends to resemble in some ways other businesses in one particular sense. Very often it tends to be a branch plant type of operation, as is the automotive industry or the plastics and chemicals industry. We find that such businesses do not appear before FIRA. They do not seek the permission of the Government to take over an existing business or to establish a new enterprise.
It should not be surprising, and it is a fact, that organized crime has a type of branch plant mentality in a great many cases. While in other areas of life we may want to encourage the development of indigenous Canadian businesses, I think in the case of organized crime we are interested in detection, in arrest and in prosecution of the branch plant nature of such operations. More so than with other crimes in Canada which are indigenous we can work in co-operation with other good, effective police forces in other countries to identify the kingpins and the agents who are involved in the operation to bring them to justice.
I want to express some criticism now of the failure of the Government to deal with the area of developing Criminal Code responses to organized crime in Canada. This is basically
Organized Crime
covered by the third and fourth parts of the Hon. Member's motion, but more particularly in part No. 4. What I think is needed are more tools to fight organized crime. When the Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Mulroney) identified drugs as an epidemic in Canada, I thought what he might do to validate the expression of such a concern is to bring forward a number of new legislative tools for fighting organized crime. The most obvious example, something that we have in Canada in only a very preliminary and modest way in the Criminal Code, is the RICO legislation which is in effect in the United States. RICO is an acronym for Racketeer Influenced Corrupt Organization.
In the United States when an organized criminal or kingpin in crime is found, new legislation enables prosecutors to go after not only the criminal assets that are used in a criminal business but other assets that have been purchased with the proceeds of such crime, including other businesses. Perhaps we have all read of the American endeavour to take over by law enforcement agencies bakeries, laundries, airplanes, boats and so on used only very peripherally, if at all, in connection with a criminal operation but purchased with the proceeds of organized crime, and to take over, in particular, bank accounts. In Canada, bank accounts have a sanctity which in some ways is larger and more holy than bank accounts in Switzerland or in the West Indies. I know that bankers in this country are good Canadians who want to comply with the laws of the land and who do comply with our laws. However, I think they could benefit, and it would assist them in preventing organized crime from using banks and exploiting their facilities, if there were an easier way than there is at present in the law to seize a bank account when a certain level of evidence can be given that organized crime is responsible for the money in the account, that it is used in crime or derived from it.
I wish to see this debate move forward. I know there are other Hon. Members who wish to speak. Therefore, I would like at this time to move an amendment to the motion by adding at the end thereof the following:
"and that the Royal Commission report back within six months of its
appointment."

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is to be commended for her interest in the extent to which organized criminal conspiracies are at work in Canada today. I am certainly pleased to speak in favour of her motion. The Hon. Member is a Member whom I have come to know over the last two and a half years in the House of Commons through a committee on which we serve. I have a lot of respect for the work that she does here in the House of Commons.

May 4, 1987
Organized Crime
I have considered the remarks and views advanced by Members of the Elouse when the matter was first discussed on March 12 last. Organized crime can be compared to a cancer intruding into the body of Canadian society. As was noted previously, the activities attributed to criminal organizations have taken many forms in the past and can be expected to continue to exploit and prey upon the weak and easily corrupted. I do not believe that any in this Elouse would doubt that the influence of organized criminal activity permeates throughout Canadian society. No part of Canada is immune to its tentacles. The presence of narcotics in the Far North is clear evidence of this. Through such activities as drug trafficking, the leeches of the criminal world are sucking the life-blood from our youth and ruining the lives of their loved ones.
Canadians are a strong and virtuous people. They may be surprised to learn to what extent organized crime has spread through the body of our society. It is indeed unfortunate that so many have been seduced by the lure of wealth and high living as portrayed in such media creations as Miami Vice to believe that they too might consider participating in such endeavours. The glamour is a fantasy. The reality is the suffering of exploited victims, the suffering of families, the suffering of those within the criminal organizations who serve those at the top of the pyramid.
An individual involved in organized crime today is likely to be outfitted in a grey business suit and his or her influence is likely to be as far-reaching as that of an important industrialist. He or she is not likely to be flamboyant and would be largely invisible to his or her fellow Canadian, but that makes his or her power for evil even greater.
The financial cost of organized crime is not limited to the vast illicit profits made through drug trafficking. When these people worm their way into legitimate businesses, the cost is borne by the public. One of the reasons for flourishing criminality is the lack of awareness on the part of the general public. The public is often the innocent accomplice of criminal schemes.
If the purpose of the proposed royal commission would be to highlight the efforts of the police, courts and others dedicated to fighting crime as well as to expose the true dimensions of organized crime so that illegal activities are unmasked, then there might be some positive results from the exercise. It may well be that the general public would learn things that are at present only known by criminal justice officials. Perhaps this information could be relied upon to support the passage of legislation required to combat organized crime in Canada. As well, it might be that a heightened awareness would enable Canadians to do what they can on an individual level to reduce the profitability of organized crime.
I was greatly impressed with what the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills (Mr. Thacker) said on March 12 of this year with regard to the number and variety of areas in which the present Government is actually moving, both internationally and on the domestic front, to deal effectively with the threat posed to Canada by organized crime. As was stated during the
first reading debate, there is already considerable movement at the federal level with officials of the Department of Justice and the Ministry of the Solicitor General discussing possible initiatives with their provincial counterparts. The task of improving the existing legislation while enhancing the capabilities of law enforcement agencies is well under way, and it is for this reason that I question the need for such a royal commission at this time.
I would like to caution both the Department of Justice and the Ministry of the Solicitor General to waste no time making these changes. I think the Canadian public is growing very impatient. The Archambault report was handed down a matter of four weeks ago and I read it with interest because of the capital punishment debate which is now going on in the House of Commons. The report says in essence that Canadians have lost confidence in the justice and penal systems. The systems have no credibility. Too many people are going to prison for minor crimes but not enough people who commit serious crimes are given sentences that really mean what they say. Too many people are being paroled from prisons when in fact they should probably be receiving longer sentences and serving full sentences. I say in not too light a vein that the justice and penal systems should certainly be reviewed with the greatest of haste.
By way of conclusion, I put forward my belief that all Hon. Members of the House appreciate the great concern over the extent of organized criminal activity in Canada voiced by the Hon. Member for Trinity. Further, we share her desire to see the Canadian criminal justice system rendered into an effective means of addressing this problem. It has been a pleasure for me to speak on today's Private Members' Motion because, as I said a moment ago, I think it relates very much to many other issues we are discussing in the House of Commons at this time and particularly to the whole issue of the justice system which I feel should certainly be reviewed.

subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   ORGANIZED CRIME ESTABLISHMENT OF ROYAL COMMISSION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would suggest that the motion is well intentioned because nobody in Canada is in favour of organized crime. Quite the contrary, all of us would want any kind of crime, not only organized crime but any crime whatever disappear from the life of Canadians, all the more so of course when we are dealing with an organization which implies constant premeditation, therefore a crime we want to fight against with even more dedication. The Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) is sponsoring a motion urging the House and recommending to the Government that a royal commission be appointed to investigate organized crime, a well intentioned motion if I ever heard one. However this raises a number of other problems because speaking of a royal investigation commission, Mr. Speaker, we have had some on other subjects, including at the provincial level. In Quebec, for example, the Commission of Inquiry on Organized Crime or the other one on tainted meat immediately springs to mind, but they did create rather serious problems for society.
May 4, 1987

A royal commission of inquiry is a very expensive tool. Today I note that the Liberal Member who spoke proposed an amendment to the motion of his colleague so that the royal commission of inquiry would complete its work within six months. I can understand why they would amend their own motion, precisely because they know full well that most of the time a royal commission of inquiry moves very slowly and takes years before producing a report. So in that sense one is justified to wonder whether it is the best way to fight against crime or against organized crime.
The process of that royal Commission is extremely costly and time consuming, as well as highly contentious because it ignores in most cases some of the basic rules of evidence which Canadians take pride in, which are traditional rules in our whole legal system and are used to protect people, to uphold the most basic rights of people, namely that anyone is deemed innocent and that no one can be declared guilty unless he has been deemed innocent in the first place. However, when a Royal Commission inquires into organized crime, for instance, it attracts so much public attention that anyone who is summoned to testify before that commission is indicted by the people without being given an opportunity to defend himself, to take advantage of the rules governing evidence which are provided in the Canadian legislation and the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms. I therefore think, Mr. Speaker, that we should have some second thoughts about this before we decide to support the establishment of such a Royal Inquiry commission.
Moreover, and 1 read again paragraphe 5 of the motion, the Royal Enquiry Commission, according to the Liberal member, should include in its report observations and recommendations on:
5. effective and appropriate punishsment in instances of organized crime
murder conspiracy;
As you know, Mr. Speaker, such a statement is totally irrelevant in a motion because if there is evidence that people, whether they belong to organized crime or not-this distinction is irrelevant again-have conspired to commit murders, if such evidence is in the hands of our police departments, there is no need for a Royal commission: Let those people be charged right away under the Criminal Code, without waiting six months, a year, or two years before they are charged and taken into custody. It is not clear what the Liberal member is attempting to do with this Royal commission of Inquiry. If she has evidence that people, whether they belong to organized crime or other associations, have conspired to commit murders, let them be indicted and sentenced, but let that happen now, and not in two years time.
Mr. Speaker, as several members mentioned earlier, organized crime derives its profits mostly from the sale of narcotics. It is everybody's secret, as you know, and it is also a well-known fact that criminals are usually engaged in criminal activities because there is some profit to be derived, and when
Organized Crime
a profit is at hand, criminals get organized to derive even greater profits. However, Mr. Speaker, although we do agree that the problem lies with the sale of narcotics, we should also agree that Canadian police forces have a number of efficient strategies at their disposal to deal with the sale and traffic of narcotics.
Let me just mention off the cuff a few of those instruments that are in the hands of police forces, to show that there is no need for a Royal Inquiry commission to tell us again what is already being done at the present time. Electronic eavesdropping exists and we use it, although it could possibly be used more. All police forces in Canada, even undercover agents, Mr. Speaker can use it. I am a lawyer, and I have seen on many occasions, during proceedings, that entire organizations had been destroyed through the use of undercover RCMP officers! Information obtained from repentant criminals allows also the police to make some good hauls. We could probably improve somewhat the means given to the police. If those who have the legal means to stop drug trafficking had more money, they could increase electronic surveillance, raise the number of officers to be trained as undercover agents and also the number of border guards.
My riding has 200 kilometres of border. Do you know how many RCMP officers there are to cover these 200 kilometres? Only three. How can they be blamed if they let some drug enter Canada! Here is an area where we could act.
One of the things which have been suggested and that the Government will probably propose in the next few weeks or months is to seize the profits from crime. If you do that, you undermine the foundations of organized crime. We could also, Mr. Speaker, and I am in favour of it, increase the sentences. We could raise the minimum prison term to seven years for importation of drugs into Canada, as we have seen that it can be effective.
The importer will know that he will not have a smile from the judge, he will not be given a reprimand, he will not be put on probation, he will not be fined, he will not get a month in jail. If he imports drugs into Canada he will get a seven-year prison term. If we were going to do the same for all drug related crimes, Mr. Speaker, we would see a lowering of the rate of that type of crime.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member for Burnaby (Mr. Robinson) mentioned the efforts I have made to abolish contributions to political parties. I thank him for his kind words, but I do not see the connection with organized crime. But even so I want to take this opportunity, Mr. Speaker, to tell him that I thank him for supporting the efforts that I make. However, I must stress that these efforts were to the effect of preventing not only corporations or associations but unions as well from making contributions to any political group. And God knows how many such contributions the New Democratic Party receives from unions, from labour organizations.

May 4, 1987
Patent Act
So, rather than bringing up that point in a debate that does not concern that, I suggest the Hon. Member should talk his own party into approving the propositions that I have always advocated.
Mr. Speaker, the motion put forward by the member for Trinity is based on a very good intention, but the means that she proposes is certainly not the best, at this time, to fight organized crime.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with considerable interest that I take part in today's debate. Although I am not a lawyer, a criminologist or a former police officer, I take part with great interest in this debate and I wish to congratulate the Hon. Member for Trinity (Miss Nicholson) for her initiative. I hold this Hon. Member in high esteem, having learned to appreciate her as a member of the public accounts committee of which she is the chairperson and where she does an excellent job.
Moreover, I wish to indicate that as a member of our Standing Committee on Private Members' Business, I received this motion which much interest, just as the other committee members did. There is a wide concensus to allow the House to debate this motion as moved.
Yet, I wish to take this opportunity to indicate that I am against appointing a Royal Commission to investigate organized crime for several reasons, the first of which being that if we held a poll or a referendum from coast to coast to know whether Canadians are in favour of appointing and financing such a Royal commission of Inquiry on organized crime, my impression is that most Canadians would not support it. When we realize the costs . . . the fact is that past Royal commissions have involved enormous costs. Most of the time, these costs amount to several millions of dollars, and for what result, Mr. Speaker? As my friend the Hon. Member for Charlevoix (Mr. Hamelin) said a while ago, they unfortunately end up being shelved without any follow-up.
We can easily imagine the reaction of the Canadian public to such an investigation. We would give them the impression that they are not properly protected against organized crime and that nothing is being done in this country.
In my opinion, there are many Hon. Members who think that there is no evidence that organized crime is more widespread than five or 10 years ago. If one thing is sure, Mr. Speaker, it is that our police forces, whether at the federal, provincial or municipal level, are now better organized and have more sophisticated means to fight against organized crime.
Mr. Speaker, regularly in the headlines and in the newspapers we read about the successful raids of our police force and I think we should now take advantage of this occasion to show them how grateful we really are for fighting against organized crime with such dedication.
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian people could be left with the impression that nothing is being done when in fact it simply is not the case. I believe that our police officers are quite efficient in their fight against organized crime. We will not find the solution there. I see that my time is over. I think that our Criminal Code should be amended and that our courts should come down a lot harder on criminals.
